entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 11: One Feature at a Time — How to Split Your Prompts
entry.content:
Intro

Yesterday we finally finished our first feature: "add an expense."

But... is that it? Nope. Next we're going to iterate on features and have the AI finish off the rest for us.

Sure, you could do it in one line: "Please read @SPEC.md and build all the remaining features."

But I really don't recommend that. It makes it easy to lose track of what it changed, and when something breaks, it's hard to trace and debug. You end up spending way more energy hunting down problems instead of focusing on building features.

So today's focus isn't really the features themselves. It's splitting the build into three rounds, with each round getting a clear prompt that tells the AI exactly how to build something that fits what you need.

Three parts of a good prompt

Personally, I think a good feature prompt has three parts:

  1. Current state: clearly describe what's on the screen right now and which part you want to change this time.
  2. What you want: what's the goal this round, and what are the specific fields and behaviors?
  3. Acceptance criteria: how do you know it's done right?

It might be a little hard at first to see why these three parts make for good feature work. Basically, all three are there to prevent one thing:

Stopping the AI from filling in too many blanks on its own, so its idea doesn't drift too far from yours.

AI is really smart these days, but sometimes it's a little too clever for its own good. So you have to describe what you want clearly, and then the AI can build something that actually fits.

There's one more thing I want to point out, and it's about "current state."

Current state just means describing what you can see and what's happening right now, like...

  • Something on the screen looks off.
  • A button doesn't do anything when you click it.

You don't need to go dig up which folder the code lives in or what the file is called. That's not the Vibe Coding spirit at all — your job is to guide the AI toward the feature you want.

For the AI, the project is right in front of it. It'll read it on its own, and it'll find the file even if you can't name it. The real problem is the other way around:

It can't see the picture in your head. That's the part worth spending your effort describing.

With that out of the way, let's see these three parts in action.

Round one: category breakdown

First, build a good habit: whenever you start a "new feature," type /clear so you're working on a clean desk. That keeps earlier discussions and build steps from affecting this round. That influence is what we call "noise."

Once the desk is clean, we're ready for the first round.

After yesterday's "add an expense," the home page already shows this month's total and a list of this month's entries, so you know how much you've spent this month:

But an expense tracker can't be that bare-bones, right? A total and a list alone still don't make it easy to see where the money actually went. So next we're building a "category breakdown," so users can see clearly which categories their money goes to.

We're going to build the "category breakdown" from SPEC.md. Here's how I'd write the prompt (don't forget to turn on Plan Mode before sending it):

The home page currently shows this month's total and this month's entries, but I can't tell which category I'm spending the most on.

Please read the "Category breakdown" part of section 5.1 in SPEC.md and build it. For placement, refer to the wireframe near the top of SPEC.md (below the total, above the list).

Acceptance criteria:

1. If this month I record Food 120, Food 80, and Transport 100, the screen should show two horizontal bars: Food $200 on top, Transport $100 below, with the Food bar longer
2. Categories with no spending this month shouldn't show up — no row of zeros
3. Round percentages to whole numbers. If three categories each have 100, show 33%, 33%, 33%. Adding up to 99% is fine, don't force it to 100%
4. Last month's data isn't included in the calculation

That prompt is really just the three parts:

  1. Current state: the home page has this month's total and entries, but I can't tell which category I'm spending the most on.
  2. What you want: add a row of category breakdown bars below the total.
  3. Acceptance criteria: four checks.

Notice I never said "please change this file or that component." We let the AI figure that out. What matters is telling it what you want the screen to look like. And if there's anything it's not sure about (like styling), it'll still ask you:

The Plan Mode plan is long, but you don't need to read every word. Just focus on three things:

  • Which files is it going to touch?
  • What's it not doing?
  • What are the acceptance criteria?

The rest? Skim it so you get the general idea.

If it all looks fine, go ahead and click "Yes, and use auto mode" and let it get to work.

You'll notice that after you approve it, it doesn't start changing code right away. It first produces docs/plans/02-category-breakdown.md. That's the rule we added to CLAUDE.md yesterday kicking in, so from today on you don't need to remind it anymore.

And finally, there's our category breakdown, built and working:

Round two: edit and delete (with a bug left in on purpose)

With the category breakdown done, round two is editing and deleting entries. Sometimes we log the wrong thing or type the wrong amount, so this one really matters.

By now you should know what to do before starting the next round: type /clear first so you have a clean desk.

Then switch to Plan Mode and try something like this prompt for round two:

Right now, clicking an item in the list on the home page does nothing. Please read "Transaction list" in section 5.1 and "Delete" in section 5.3 of SPEC.md.

When the user clicks any item in the list, open an edit form. The form shows four fields, pre-filled with that item's existing data. When the user finishes editing and clicks save, the form closes. The edit form also needs a "Delete" button; clicking it shows a confirmation prompt, and once the user confirms, that item is deleted and the form closes.

One more thing: I want you to deliberately set up a controlled debugging exercise. On purpose, use "which position this item is in the list on screen" to identify the item for editing and deleting — don't use each item's id. Add the comment "TODO for later practice: switch to id" next to the related code, and don't fix it to use id yet.

Acceptance criteria: add three expenses on the same day in a row. Clicking the middle one opens the edit form, clicking delete shows a delete confirmation, and after a successful delete the form closes and only the middle item disappears from the home page list. If you click cancel, nothing changes.

Along the way, it'll probably ask you how to build the popup:

Same as before, you can just go with "recommended" unless you have other ideas.

I need to explain something here. Normally, deleting by index isn't a good approach. This is a known bug I designed on purpose — the right way is to use an id (a unique value). The AI would normally fix this on its own, which is why we have to specifically tell it to make the mistake.

If the difference between index and id doesn't quite click, here's an example: say there are 30 students in a class, and you take attendance by "the Nth student." If they secretly swap seats, you'll have a hard time calling the right person. Think of an id as the student's ID number or name — even if they swap seats, you'll still get the right person.

Once that makes sense, you should get this Plan Mode plan. Same deal: if it looks fine, click "Yes, and use auto mode" and let the AI build it.

Why set up a scenario like this? You're probably wondering. It's to let you experience one thing for yourself:

Passing review doesn't mean there are no bugs. It just means you didn't happen to test that scenario.

After the AI finishes, tell it:

Please commit the current progress with the message: "Practice: edit and delete, index bug left in"

That way, when you (or the AI) go bug hunting later, you'll know this version has a bug in it.

You might have noticed this message doesn't follow the "Feature name: short description" format we set in CLAUDE.md. That's on purpose. Starting it with "Practice:" means you can spot this teaching landmine in the git history at a glance, and it won't get mixed up with normal feature commits.

Round three: switching months

Round three works pretty much the same as the first two. /clear first, switch to Plan Mode, then try something like this prompt:

The top of the home page is currently stuck on this month, and there's no way to see other months' data.

Please read "Month switching" in section 5.1 of SPEC.md. Add an arrow on each side of the year/month line to switch to the previous/next month, plus a "This month" button to jump straight back.

Acceptance criteria: press the left arrow repeatedly to go back three months, and the total, category breakdown, and list should all switch to that month's data. Then click "This month" once to go straight back to the current month. After coming back, the "This month" button disappears, but the left and right arrows don't shift position because of it.

The process is pretty much the same as the first two rounds, so I won't repeat it.

After finishing month switching, these three rounds should leave you with a pretty strong feel for why "one feature at a time" works so well.

flowchart LR
    A["/clear to start a new conversation"] --> B["Switch to Plan Mode"]
    B --> C["Prompt with three parts<br>current state, what you want, acceptance criteria"]
    C --> D["Read the plan, approve only if it looks right"]
    D --> E["AI Agent builds the feature"]
    E --> F{"Review against acceptance criteria"}
    F -->|"Pass"| G["Commit to save"]
    F -->|"Fail"| H["Describe the gap/problem, ask AI to fix it"]
    H --> E
    G --> A

Why type /clear every time?

Across these three rounds, I kept stressing that you should /clear first.

That ties back to the Context Window idea from Day 6 (a desk with limited space). Whatever the AI Agent built earlier (the Context) can pollute what comes next. So usually, every time we start a new round of work, we /clear once so the previous round doesn't affect the current one.

So does our project's shared understanding get wiped? Nope.

When you run /clear, the AI does clean off its desk, but it also puts CLAUDE.md back on it. Then when you start the next round, it works from what's in CLAUDE.md (and pulls in SPEC.md too), so the previous round doesn't bleed into the current one.

So you can use /clear with total peace of mind.

Just to be clear, "one feature at a time" doesn't mean chopping features up as fine as pickles. Aim for a size you can "finish in one go and review at a glance." The category breakdown is one round, edit and delete is one round, but "the color of the delete button" doesn't need its own round — just handle it as part of that round.

If you've been following along exactly, your git history should now have a "Practice: edit and delete, index bug left in" commit. That's the only landmine in the whole series that gets to survive overnight. Tomorrow we'll set it off and then fix it.

Wrapping up

We've finally made it to Day 11. Today we ran three rounds of feature work, all using the same approach:

  1. /clear to clean the desk (start a new conversation), switch to Plan Mode, describe what you need using the three prompt parts (current state, what you want, acceptance criteria), read the plan before approving, review against the criteria when it's done, and commit once it passes.
  2. Start every round in Plan Mode. The plans might be long, but as the project's foundation gets more solid, there's less and less you need to read.
  3. Don't be afraid of /clear wiping important info. Every clear puts CLAUDE.md back in, and the shared understanding that really needs to stick around is already written into SPEC.md and CLAUDE.md.

At this point we've finished all six items on the "In" list in section 3 of SPEC.md. The expense tracker app can now "add, edit, delete, and switch months," and the data gets saved.

But there's still that landmine we planted in the project. Tomorrow we'll walk through a full bug-fixing session live, so hold off on sneaking in a fix before then.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 10: Building the First Feature with Plan Mode
entry.content:
Intro

SPEC.md, CLAUDE.md, the project environment — that's all pretty much done. Now we finally get to start actually building!

The first feature on the list is "add an expense." Since it's the very first feature in the whole project, we'll use it to show how to build things with Plan Mode.

Turning one feature from the SPEC into a prompt

First, let's look at the "Scope" section in SPEC.md:

## 3. Scope

### In

- Add an expense
- Edit a recorded expense
- Delete a recorded expense
- Switch months to see that month's total spending and category breakdown
- Jump back to the current month in one tap
- See that month's transaction list

That's the list of features we "have to build." Before we start, make sure the AI is in plan mode on (remember? Just press Shift+Tab to switch) so it goes into planning mode.

Once you're in Plan Mode, we can take the first step: turning the feature list in SPEC.md into a prompt. One thing to keep in mind — in this post we're not asking the AI to build every feature in one go. We're only doing the first item on the "In" list, "Add an expense," and using it to show how Plan Mode works.

If that all sounds good, try typing this prompt into Claude Code:

Following the first item on the "In" list in SPEC.md, "Add an expense," please write a development plan. List what this round will and won't do, and include acceptance criteria.

Yep, that's it.

"Don't I need to tell it about the fields and categories? Those are the basics of an expense tracker."

I know you might be wondering that, but you really don't. We already worked all of that out while writing SPEC.md.

Don't believe me? Look — the field rules are already written out in section 5 of SPEC.md:

**Field rules**

| Field | Required | Default | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| Amount | Yes | Empty | Positive integer, must be > 0 |
| Category | Yes | None | Pick one of six, using buttons, not a dropdown |
| Date | Yes | Today | Native `<input type="date">` |
| Note | No | Empty | Single line of text, max 50 characters |

That's why I don't need to tell the AI...

  • What the fields are
  • What the categories are

We already spent time talking these through earlier, and SPEC.md has the full spec.

If you type all that out again in this prompt, you get two problems:

  1. You're writing the same thing twice, which wastes time
  2. The two might drift out of sync someday

That's why laying the groundwork up front matters so much. It's exactly why we spent the time getting SPEC.md, CLAUDE.md, and the project environment ready — so when it's time to build, we can get straight to the point.

After you hit send: it asks questions before giving you a plan

After you send that prompt, it might not hand you a plan right away. Instead, just like before, it may pop up multiple-choice questions and check things with you one at a time.

In my case, the questions were:

1. To review "Add an expense," you need to be able to see the result of adding one. Should this round also include a read-only transaction list and this month's total?
2. How far should src/composables/useRecords.js go in this round?

When you hit questions like these, that's basically your cue to stop, flip through SPEC.md, and actually think about it. These are often things you didn't think of in the first place, which is exactly why we keep building in these check steps (and if there's anything you don't understand, just ask it — better than discovering the problem halfway through building). Every option can add complexity, difficulty, or plain workload to a feature. And the stuff you left out of your prompt doesn't magically disappear — it just gets asked at a different point in time. That's the value of Plan Mode.

Understanding how it wants to build the house

Next you should see the AI hand you a development plan. I really recommend you actually read it (we'll save this plan to a file in a bit, so hang on).

Please don't just see "Yes, and use auto mode" and click it without thinking.

The plan is a bit long, but I think it's worth taking some time to read. For example, it says things like...

  • Categories are hardcoded in src/constants/categories.js as the single source of truth.
  • src/composables/useRecords.js is the only place that touches localStorage.

Just those two lines might already wear you out. There's a lot of it, and it's packed with jargon, so it's totally normal for it to feel painful to read. But you can ask it to rewrite things into a "version that's easier to understand," and it'll break the plan down in a friendlier way. Say it's your first time seeing composable — you can type this into "Tell Claude what to change":

What's a composable? Why do we need an extra useRecords.js file, and what is localStorage? Please explain it in a way that's easier to understand.

And you'll get a really detailed plain-language explanation:

After reading the explanation, you should see that it didn't split things up randomly — it made those design decisions for real reasons.

And if... you understood it, you read it all, but you just don't have an opinion either way? Then go with the "recommended" option. "Recommended" is what it thinks is the best approach, so unless you can come up with a better reason, just go with it.

For now, though, don't click "Yes, and use auto mode" yet, because we've got a "controlled failure" exercise to do first.

Controlled failure exercise: bloat the scope on purpose, then hit the brakes

Next we're going to do a "controlled failure" exercise: deliberately bloat the plan, then pull it back.

Type this into "Tell Claude what to change":

Back to the plan. Since we're building a form anyway, let's also add over-budget alerts and a way to record income.
Please update the plan, but don't execute it yet.

After sending it, again, don't rush to click "Yes, and use auto mode." Take a look at how the plan bloats first. You should also see the AI tell you something like this:

### Out (explicitly excluded from v1)

| Not doing | Why |
|---|---|
| Recording income | It only answers "where did my money go," not assets and liabilities |
| Accounts / payment methods | Adding these leads straight to "balance per account," which the MVP can't handle |
| Budgets and over-budget alerts | First get people to actually record expenses, then talk about control |
| Month-over-month trend charts | Meaningless until there are a few months of data |
| Adding / deleting / renaming categories | A fixed built-in set is enough and saves a whole management screen |
| Accounts, cloud sync, multiple devices | Single user, single device |

Pretty interesting, right? The AI actually pushes back on our request, because it knows these features aren't in scope this time. And for those of us with itchy fingers who want to keep adding features, this is the perfect chance to practice hitting the brakes. As long as you don't accept it or allow it, you're fine.

Once you've seen how scope control works and how the plan bloats, press Esc or find the "Tell Claude what to change" box and type this:

That was just a scope-control exercise. Budget alerts and income tracking are both on the "Out" list in section 3 of SPEC.md, so please remove all of them.

Go back to the original "Add an expense," list what this round will and won't do, and give me a new version of the plan.

It'll go back to the original plan, but you'll probably notice the AI adds a special note about it:

It's a tiny exercise, but it means a lot. Sometimes scope explosions aren't caused by the AI at all — it's the user suddenly thinking of something (just like a boss). The nice part here is that you hit the brakes before any work even started.

Approve it and watch it build

If the plan looks fine, click "Yes, and use auto mode" and let it run the plan. You'll see it start adding and changing files in your project until it's done (and if you'd rather see every change with your own eyes, picking manually approve is totally fine too — it's just slower).

When it's done, run npm run dev and open your browser. You should see the home page with a "+ Add" button, and after you add an expense, the bare-bones list below it will show the data.

Keep the plan

Don't jump into reviewing yet. There's one thing a lot of people forget to do first:

If you don't save that plan, it's gone.

The plan was produced inside the conversation. Once you /clear, it gets wiped along with everything else on the desk. But it's actually really useful later on, for example...

  • When a bug shows up, you can pull it out and check whether the AI actually followed the plan.
  • A few months later, you can see why the files were split up the way they were.

So tell the AI:

Please save the original text of that plan as docs/plans/01-add-expense.md. Don't rewrite or summarize it.

You really need that "don't rewrite or summarize it" part. Otherwise it'll helpfully condense the whole thing into three lines, and then there's no point in saving it (mine is at day10#docs/plans).

Once it's saved, your project will have a new folder:

money-note/
└─ docs/
   └─ plans/
      └─ 01-add-expense.md

So... do you have to say this every single time? Of course not. A convention that keeps repeating like this is exactly what CLAUDE.md is for. Send it one more prompt:

Please add the following dev rules to CLAUDE.md, and follow them in every conversation:

- Every time a Plan Mode plan is approved, the first thing to do is save the original plan text as docs/plans/NN-feature-name.md (NN starts at 01 and keeps counting up), and only start changing code after it's saved
- The plan file goes in the same commit as that feature's code

This is exactly the same move as on Day 9, when we added dev rules to CLAUDE.md. And it proves something:

CLAUDE.md isn't something you write once and never touch again. Whenever you find a convention worth keeping, add a line.

From now on, every round of feature work, it'll save the plan on its own. You won't have to tell it twice.

Reviewing the feature

Next up is review. You might be thinking...

"Wait, I have to spend time testing this myself?"

Not really. Your Plan Mode plan already listed the acceptance criteria for you — those 13 items in the plan. The first half maps to the acceptance criteria in section 7 of SPEC.md, and the second half are edge-case checks it added on its own. Every one of them is behavior you can check yourself just by opening the browser.

When the AI finishes, it'll tell you it already tested everything. Don't take its word for it just yet (why? You'll find out on Day 12). I still open it up and test by hand, especially these:

  • Tap "+" → enter an amount → tap a category → save — an expense is recorded in three steps
  • The one you just added shows up at the top of the list right away, and this month's total goes up
  • Change the date to last month and save — that one doesn't show up in this month's list

The acceptance criteria here are about "behavior," not "code." You don't need to check whether the code is written correctly — what matters is whether what it built meets the acceptance criteria.

If everything passes, the AI will ask whether you want to commit, because the "Wrap-up" section of the plan says:

Once all 13 items above pass, commit once. Message format per CLAUDE.md:

Add expense: form, data layer, and transaction list

And that rule actually comes straight from the CLAUDE.md constitution:

**Commit once each time a feature is finished and passes review.** Don't pile up several features into one commit — one commit maps to one reviewable feature, so you can go back when something breaks.

Wrapping up

That's about it for today. Congrats on finishing your first feature.

You've probably noticed by now that even though Vibe Coding is an AI-driven way of building, it's not fully automatic. You still need to think, make judgment calls, and review, so the features you end up with actually match what you need.

Here's the rhythm of the whole process, so you can refer back to it when building other features:

  1. Your prompt just needs to point at which feature in SPEC.md you're building, then ask it to list what it will and won't do this round, with acceptance criteria. Don't keep feeding it new rules that could conflict with SPEC.md
  2. If it asks you questions, stop and think. Go back and check SPEC.md too — every option affects how much work comes later
  3. If there's anything in the plan you don't understand, just ask. Keep asking until you get it
  4. Once you have the plan, read it through properly, especially the data structure parts
  5. If you notice the scope growing — whether the AI suggested it or you thought of it on the spot — send it back and have it re-plan
  6. Save the plan as docs/plans/NN-feature-name.md, and put that convention in CLAUDE.md so you never have to ask again
  7. When reviewing, look at behavior, not code. Only commit after everything passes

Following these seven steps, you're already slowly building your own Vibe Coding workflow.

That's it for today. Congrats on your project's very first commit, and I hope this post helped you get your first feature done.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 9: Setting Up the Project with CLAUDE.md and git init
entry.content:
Intro

"SPEC.md is done, so I can finally tell the AI to start writing code, right?!"

Hold on. If you think a finished SPEC.md means you can jump straight into "go build it," that's the wrong idea and the wrong process.

So don't grab your SPEC.md and run off to the AI just yet.

It already picked your tech stack. Did you agree to it?

First things first: if we're building an expense tracker app, we have to decide what tech to build it with. But as non-engineers, how are we supposed to know what Vue, React, Svelte, Angular, Next.js, Nuxt... all these names even mean?

Don't panic. Open yesterday's SPEC.md (you can check the example file on GitHub #day9) and scroll down to section 6, "Tech decisions." You'll notice something interesting:

While Claude was interviewing you, it quietly went ahead and picked the tech for you.

Things like Vue 3 + Vite, Tailwind CSS, no Router, no Pinia — it even thought through the file structure. But here's the question... did you ever agree to that? Do you even know what those things are?

AI is smart, but it can also be a bit of a busybody. And that busybody streak is exactly how "AI amplifies your vagueness" comes true. In the last post we were turning an idea into a spec — we never talked about tech choices at all. But the AI figured it might as well get that ready for you, and you happened not to notice what it picked. So now SPEC.md has a tech decision baked in.

To be fair, the decision isn't necessarily wrong (you'll see in a minute that it actually picked pretty well). But "the AI decided" and "you signed off" are two different things. So today we're going to make that call properly and lock in the tech stack.

Go into the money-note folder, start claude, and type:

Please read SPEC.md.
Based on this spec, what tech would be the best fit?
Give me two or three options, explain the pros and cons of each, and then give me your recommendation.

A few things matter to me. I want it to be...

- Simple enough
- Mainstream enough
- Easy to deploy

If you're worried the AI will skim or misread things, you can ask it: "What's in the SPEC.md file in this project? List its section headings first, then explain what's in it." That way you can confirm it actually read SPEC.md.

Here's the fun part: it labels the original choice from SPEC as "Option A (SPEC's original plan)" on its own, and only then gives you alternatives. In my conversation it came up with three:

  • Option A: Vue 3 + Vite + Tailwind (SPEC's original plan)
  • Option B: Plain HTML + JS + CSS, single file, no build step
  • Option C: React + Vite + Tailwind

And in its write-up you'll spot a couple of key points:

  1. This app has no need for a server at all
  2. How much help you need with reactivity

At this point I bet you're full of questions. What does "how much help you need with reactivity" even mean? The trick hasn't changed — just ask the AI to explain it in plain language:

I don't understand "how much help you need with reactivity." Can you explain it in plain language?

It'll tell you that "reactivity" means "when the data changes, the screen updates automatically."

The screenshot is from a Chinese conversation, where the AI picked a slightly unusual word for "reactive." That's just a quirk of its training data — don't worry about it. What matters is that it explained the idea clearly.

After reading all that, I'd still recommend keeping the original plan, unless you want to challenge yourself with a different stack. Use this prompt to have the AI add a decision log entry:

I've decided to keep Option A (SPEC's original plan): Vue 3 + Vite + Tailwind.
Please add this entry to the "Decision log" in SPEC.md: the tech stack stays as originally planned, confirmed after comparing it with plain HTML and React. Don't change anything else.

Writing decisions down will absolutely help you when you look back in a few days, a few months, or even a few years. These are some of the most valuable assets in your project.

The options it lists also take your past conversations and background into account (it knows I write Vue all the time), so the options and reasons you see might differ from mine. That's totally normal. The point isn't to copy my answer — it's to actually understand the reasons it gives you before you say yes. If you're not building an expense tracker, the process is the same: hand over the spec, ask for options, read the reasons. Different requirements will land on different answers.

So that's our stack settled: Vue 3 + Vite for the UI, Tailwind for styling, and LocalStorage for saving data. As for where to deploy it... we'll get to that in a later post.

Getting your environment ready

Think you can start building now? Nope. Next up is the dev environment.

Honestly, I think this is where a lot of beginners get stuck, because you have to install an extra program: Node.js.

Open the official Node.js download page and grab the LTS version (Long Term Support — just click the button marked LTS; if the version number is newer than in my screenshot, that's normal).

Node.js download page: https://nodejs.org/en/download

Then pick whichever install method you like. I won't go into detail here since Windows, macOS, and Linux are all a bit different — just follow the instructions on screen.

On top of that, you'll need to install git (the version control tool):

Git download page: https://git-scm.com/downloads

Before we start, we need to check that these tools are actually installed. "Installed but not working" is where beginners die the most.

Open your terminal (if you're still inside Claude Code, type /exit first, or just open a new terminal window) and run each of these:

Check your Node.js version:

node -v

Check your npm version:

npm -v

Check your git version:

git --version

There's really only one thing that matters: all three commands should output a version number.

If any of them does nothing or throws an error, copy the command you ran along with the full error message and ask claude.ai. For environment problems like this, pasting the complete message usually gets you a fix pretty fast. Sort it out before moving on, because everything after this depends on these three.

Finally, I strongly recommend installing the Claude in Chrome extension for your browser. Later on it lets the AI drive your browser to debug things, so it's worth setting up ahead of time.

Let the AI set up the dev environment

So what now? Do we have to type a bunch of commands like an engineer? Nope.

Just tell the AI:

Based on the spec in SPEC.md, please set up the development environment for me. Don't start building features yet.

Yep, it's that simple. The AI will probably ask you a few questions along the way.

I often add "don't start building features yet" on purpose, because the AI loves to be helpful and jump straight into coding before your environment is even ready, which makes mistakes a lot more likely.

Once it's done, your folder will have a bunch of new stuff in it (package.json, src/, node_modules, and so on). That's the skeleton of a Vue project. You don't need to get to know each of them right now — I'll introduce them as they come up.

When it's ready, tell the AI:

Please start the project's dev server. I want to preview the project.

The AI should tell you it has started the dev server and give you a URL. For Vue it's usually http://localhost:5173/ (it might be different, so go with whatever URL the AI gives you). Paste that URL into your browser to see the project.

Different tech stacks start their dev servers in different ways, but it almost always ends with a URL you can open in your browser to see the project.

And with that, the basic environment is sorted.

git init: the undo button for Vibe Coding

Next, let me talk a bit about something really important in Vibe Coding — call it an undo button, or a time machine: Git.

I think Git is the single most important tool in any Vibe Coding project, and it's something you really have to get comfortable with. You don't need to keep typing commands like an engineer does:

git init
git add -A
git commit -m "Feature name: short description"

But you're going to really need its "undo button" and "time machine" powers.

What do I mean? Back in Day 4's wrap-up I said: "If you regret a change, use /rewind (or press Esc twice), but keep in mind it can't undo changes made through Bash." So once the AI runs a bash command, /rewind can't save you. Git can, because everything gets recorded in commits, and you can jump back to whichever version you want.

Think of a "commit" as a save point in a video game. Every commit is a complete save, and you can go back to any of them.

So what do we need to do with Git? Nothing, actually.

The person running these commands is the AI, not us humans. All you need to do is make sure Git is installed and tell the AI:

Please make sure to initialize my code with git init.

And you're set.

Heads up: today we're only doing the "initialize" part. We haven't made any commits (save points) yet. The first save point shows up tomorrow, after we finish the first feature and it passes review. That also lines up with the dev rule we're about to put in CLAUDE.md: only commit after a feature passes review.

The AI's constitution: CLAUDE.md

Last thing for today — we need to meet CLAUDE.md.

This thing is really, really, really important. Why? Pretty simple: CLAUDE.md gets loaded automatically into every conversation. It's like the project's constitution, holding the project's rules, tech stack, command conventions, and so on.

In earlier posts, whenever we typed /clear or opened a new conversation, all the settings we wanted would just disappear. But with CLAUDE.md, the settings and rules you want, like...

- Always reply in English
- ...

...get loaded back in automatically, so you don't run into the "it forgot my settings" problem anymore.

It's a good idea to keep CLAUDE.md under 250 lines, and to put in rules the AI can't figure out just by reading the code — things like "always reply in English."

Creating one is simple, and there are usually two ways:

  • Create it manually: add a file named CLAUDE.md in the project root and write your rules in it.
  • Use the built-in /init command: it scans your project and generates a CLAUDE.md automatically. The generated version mostly describes how things are right now, so we'll add the "dev rules" ourselves.

Which is better? If you're a total beginner, I'd just use /init — it's easier. If you've got some experience, creating it by hand gives you more precise control over what goes in.

Here's the CLAUDE.md that /init generated for me, for reference (day9#CLAUDE.md). Mine is in Chinese, but you'll most likely get an English one out of the box, so you can use it as is.

There's one more small tweak to make: defining a simple dev workflow. Just send this prompt to the AI:

Please add the following dev rules to CLAUDE.md, and follow them in every conversation:

- Commit once each time a feature passes review, using the commit message format "Feature name: short description"
- Write commit messages in English

Today's mini challenge

As usual, here's a small challenge. Try to confirm the following:

  • node -v, npm -v, and git --version all show a version number.
  • Ask the AI to start the server, and you can see the page in your browser instead of "This site can't be reached" or an error screen.
  • SPEC.md and CLAUDE.md both live in the root of money-note/.

Pretty easy, right? If something goes wrong, go back through the earlier sections, or take a screenshot and ask the AI. It can usually sort it out for you.

Wrapping up

Let's recap what we did today.

It's basically like driving in the foundation piles. We did three key things:

  1. Tech choices: even when the AI picks for you, lay the options out, understand the reasons, and then officially sign off. Being mainstream is a real plus for Vibe Coding.
  2. git init: a really important undo button and time machine.
  3. CLAUDE.md: the project constitution. Put in the rules the AI can't learn just by reading the code, and it gets loaded automatically in every conversation.

That's it for today. See you tomorrow.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 8: Turning Ideas into a Spec — Writing SPEC.md with AI
entry.content:
Intro

Starting today, we're pretty much getting ready to build. We've already sorted out the AI concepts and the little details of using Claude Code, so naturally it's time to move into the implementation phase.

But! Even though we're heading into implementation, we still won't write a single line of code today. The first step of Vibe Coding isn't telling the AI to write code. It's learning to explain what you actually want.

By getting your "requirements" clear, you can turn a fuzzy idea in your head into a concrete spec document, SPEC.md. But how to get your requirements clear is a whole different story. So this post covers some techniques to squeeze that fuzzy idea into a concrete SPEC.md as much as possible, so the AI doesn't fill in the blanks on its own and hand you something that's heading who-knows-where.

AI amplifies your vagueness

First, there's one thing I think you need to accept:

AI is super convenient, but if you don't make your requirements clear, different models will fill in the gaps in noticeably different ways.

Models differ in training data, training methods, model size, and parameters, so they'll interpret the same prompt differently. Even the same model can behave differently at different points in time.

Let's use the small expense tracker we'll be building later as an example (the project folder will be called money-note).

Say you just tell the AI "build me an expense tracker app." Have you thought about how the AI will interpret that?

  • Does it need money transfers?
  • Does it need cloud sharing?
  • Where should the data be stored?
  • Does it need login?
  • Does it need to store user data?

When the AI runs into requirements it's unsure about, it'll pop up a multiple-choice screen like this and ask you:

Those questions showing up means the AI finds the request really unclear. So the AI tells itself, "I think I should ask the user what they need," and throws these options at you to pick from.

The more room you leave it to guess, the further the final product will drift from what you imagined. You might even get features you never wanted. That's why we need to make the requirements clear first, so the AI doesn't fill in the blanks on its own.

It's just like talking to an engineer. If all you say is "build me an expense tracker app," the engineer is going to ask you a ton of questions too, because they don't know what you need either.

Let the AI guide you through building the spec

After all that, have you ever wondered what a "spec" actually is?

In short, a spec is a product specification document. It lays out in detail the features you want, the features you don't want, and how to check whether the project counts as done.

But here's the problem: for a total newbie like me, how are you even supposed to write one? We don't have the background, and we're not Product Managers either, so sorting out requirements is definitely going to feel like a struggle.

So this is where we lean on working with AI. We'll have it help us turn the fuzzy idea in our heads into a concrete SPEC.md.

First, open your terminal and run these commands to create the project folder (same as the claude-playground one from before):

mkdir money-note # create the project folder
cd money-note # go into the project folder
claude # start Claude Code

Once you're in Claude Code (don't forget to use Shift+Tab to switch to manual mode, the default mode), we'll use a style of asking I call the "interview-style prompt". This Prompt has three key points:

  1. Tell the AI clearly not to write any code yet, so it doesn't get overeager and start building.
  2. Have it ask only one question at a time, so it doesn't throw ten questions at you at once and stump you. Trust me, this really is better (speaking from experience, sigh...).
  3. Once the AI thinks things are specific enough, have it organize everything into SPEC.md.

So now, copy the Prompt below, paste it into Claude Code's input box, and hit Enter:

I want to build a small expense tracking tool. Don't write any code yet.
Act as my product consultant and ask me one question at a time to clarify the requirements.
Once you think it's specific enough, tell me it's ready to be organized into SPEC.md and ask me to confirm.

Remember that AI is random. The content and options on your screen may look different from mine, but they'll generally revolve around three areas: users, feature scope, and data storage.

What follows is basically a long round of interrogation. The scope will probably cover things like:

  • What's the motivation? (I want to log expenses quickly and always know how much I've spent this month)
  • Who's using it? (Just me, single user)
  • Income or expenses? (I answered "just expenses" at the time. Remember that answer, because on Day 10 it comes back to bite me)
  • Which fields do you need? (Amount, category, date, note)
  • Where should the data be stored? Does it need to sync across devices? (Local is fine, no sync needed)
  • What stats do you want to see? (How much I spent this month, and the share by category)

...and so on.

During this process, you'll probably notice some questions you'd never even thought about. That's exactly where the value of the "interview style" comes in.

An interview-style Prompt drags out all those half-formed decisions in your head one by one, and in the end you get a complete requirements summary. If it looks fine to you, you can ask it to organize everything into SPEC.md and save it.

At this point you're probably curious: what's the difference between an "interview-style Prompt" and Plan Mode? Here's the difference:

  • Plan Mode: it's geared toward starting work once the plan is done. It produces an implementation plan (which files to touch, what steps to take), then asks whether you want to go ahead. It'll ask you questions when things are fuzzy too, but the point of those questions is always what it needs "to lock down the plan and start implementing."
  • Interview-style Prompt: it's geared toward clarifying requirements. The goal isn't to start building. It mainly produces a requirements spec, figuring out the what (what to build) first. The how (how to build it) is Plan Mode's job later. And you control the pace of the questions, since you told it to dig one question at a time instead of letting it decide when it's asked enough.

So what does the actual output look like? Here's the SPEC.md I ended up with:

  • GitHub link: day-8#SPEC.md

There are a couple of important parts in this SPEC.md: "explicitly not doing" and "features to build." These two draw the boundaries of the scope, and they're really important. Without them, there's a high chance your scope explodes and the product never gets to launch first.

Scope explosion here means building whatever pops into your head, until the project dies before the first version is even out. What a product needs most is to grab that "first-mover advantage".

One last reminder here:

A spec isn't holy scripture, and it's not set in stone.

It's a living document. As your understanding of the project gets clearer during development, the doc gets updated too. But it should basically stay within the agreed scope. If you want to add or remove features, put them under future expansion first, and update SPEC.md at the same time so the doc stays in sync with reality.

Run a scope check before you start building

Next, don't rush to hand this SPEC.md to the AI to build. Right now, this SPEC.md is just what came out of a Q&A between you and the AI, and during that process you were both in a "let's wrap this up quickly" mood. If you implement straight from it, it's really easy to miss things. So we'll ask the AI for one more "scope check."

Type /clear or /new to wipe the earlier conversation, and swap the AI's "product consultant" hat for an "inspector" hat. From a third-party angle, have it go through the spec and check three things:

Read SPEC.md, and don't change any files yet. Check three things for me:

1. Is any item in the "to build" list too vague to be checked?
2. Do any items in "to build" and "not building" contradict or overlap each other?
3. Is there any feature mentioned in the text that doesn't appear in the "to build" list?

Only report the results. Don't touch any files.

You'll see it catches a bunch of issues that haven't been decided yet. Some you can probably understand (hopefully?), like this one:

SPEC.md:112 says "no limit on how far back or forward you can switch," but there's no "back to this month" entry on screen. If a user accidentally switches to 2019, they'd have to press ▶ 80-something times to get back. Either add a "This month" button, or state in the spec that this trade-off is accepted.

For me, just adding a "This month" button solves it:

Add a "Back to this month" button to the month switcher, and add it to the "to build" list and the acceptance criteria.

This is exactly the kind of thing neither you nor the AI happened to think of, and that's why you do a scope check. You were both in a hurry to wrap up, so a lot of details slipped by.

Okay, that one's handled. But... what if some of them you just don't understand? What then? For example:

The sample data in SPEC.md:54 contradicts itself: date: "2026-08-07", but createdAt: 1754534400000 converts to 2025-08-07. That's a year off. Samples like this often get copied straight into test data or seeds.

It's fine if you don't understand it. Just don't skip it and pretend you didn't see it. You can ask the AI to explain:

Also, I don't understand this one: "The sample data in SPEC.md:54 contradicts itself: date: "2026-08-07", but createdAt: 1754534400000 converts to 2025-08-07. That's a year off." Can you explain it in plain language and suggest a correct example?

It'll explain in plain language that createdAt is a "timestamp" (one way computers record time), and that the number in the sample converts back to 2025, a year off from the 2026 above. Then it'll give you a corrected value.

At this point, let's assume everything checks out. So we lock it in with the AI like this:

Update SPEC.md based on these conclusions, and don't touch anything else.

Finally, add a "Decision Log" section at the end of the doc listing the decisions we made this time.

Trust me, keeping a decision log matters a lot. A few days from now you'll definitely forget why you decided something, and then you can just flip to this section instead of thinking it all through again.

From here on, it's your turn. Try going back and forth with the AI to clarify things and get a feel for how powerful the "interview-style Prompt" is, until you feel every feature in SPEC.md can be checked, nothing contradicts, and nothing's missing.

Later, when it's time to build your own project, the process is the same:

  • Make a call on each issue the check catches, one by one
  • Ask the AI to update SPEC.md, then run the check prompt above again after the update

Only when all three questions come back with "none" is the spec final.

I've drawn the whole flow as a chart for reference:

flowchart TD
    A["Interview-style Prompt<br>Clarify requirements one question at a time"] --> B["Produce the first SPEC.md"]
    B --> C["/clear and put on the inspector hat<br>Run the scope check Prompt"]
    C --> D{"Did it catch any issues?"}
    D -->|"Yes, and I understand them"| E["Make the call<br>Tell it your decision"]
    D -->|"Yes, but I don't understand them"| F["Ask the AI to explain in plain language<br>Decide once you get it"]
    E --> G["Ask the AI to update SPEC.md<br>and add to the decision log"]
    F --> G
    G --> C
    D -->|"All three come back 'none'"| H["SPEC.md is final<br>Ready to start building"]

Here's some homework for you:

  • Follow the flow above and create a SPEC.md that has three sections: "to build / not building / acceptance."
  • Things like account login, budget alerts, and cloud sync must be explicitly listed under "not building."

This whole process is really about forcing you to think things through. Otherwise, once you actually start building, all those fuzzy areas you didn't think through come back one by one to collect their debt. That's how scope explosions happen (and it's also why engineers are always complaining that PMs never get the requirements clear).

Wrap up

Okay, that's about time, so let's wrap up.

We didn't write a single line of code today, but we were actually working on the most important thing: "turning ideas into a spec." That's laying the foundation.

Going from knowing nothing, to having a fuzzy idea, to having a concrete spec doc used to take days in the past, sometimes even pulling in other people to help run requirements interviews. Now, with AI helping out, we can squeeze a fuzzy idea into a concrete spec in a short amount of time.

If everything here makes sense, see you in the next post.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 7: Week 1 Wrap-Up — 5 Mistakes Beginners Make Most
entry.content:
Intro

We've finally made it to the end of week one. This week we went all the way from...

  • What Vibe Coding is (Day 2)
  • Installing an AI Agent and picking a subscription plan (Day 3)
  • Your first task: reading the diff and using /rewind to take it back (Day 4)
  • Permissions and Plan Mode (Day 5)
  • Context and Tokens (Day 6)

These are all things I think you really need to understand before you start Vibe Coding.

Today is a bit lighter. We'll wrap up the first six days by going through the five most common mistakes beginners make with Vibe Coding, so you can check whether you've stepped on any of them and avoid falling into the same holes once we get into the real build.

Mistake #1: Hitting Yes on everything without reading it

Pretty much everyone steps on this one, newbie or veteran, and I'd honestly rank it number one lol.

Humans are lazy by nature. You see Yes and reflexively go Yes, Yes, Yes all the way down.

Then three days later, you have no idea what the AI changed, or even what's been happening in your project. So when a bug shows up, you have nowhere to start, and you end up burning more Tokens asking the AI "why is it broken?" and falling into the same hole again.

So how do you avoid this?

It's really just a habit. Read the diff properly the way we covered in Day 4, make sure every change is what you actually want, and only then hit Yes. If you're not confident, hit No first and tell it what you want instead.

Mistake #2: One conversation from morning to night

This is another one beginners run into constantly: doing a ton of stuff in the same Context Window, completely ignoring the Context limit, and letting the AI trigger Auto compact again and again.

The fix is pretty simple:

  • One task, one conversation. When it's done, /clear to wipe the table.
  • Get into the habit of watching Context. Run /context now and then to see how full the table is and build your own feel for it.
    • If the task isn't done yet, use /compact [what to keep] to compress the table, keep the key points, and free up space for new work.

You can pair this with Claude Code Status Line Setup: Monitor Context Usage and Rate Limit in Real-Time to watch Context usage live, so you don't only find out once the table is full. Other AI tools have similar features too.

Mistake #3: Git matters more than you think

I didn't really cover Git in the earlier posts. That's because I think bringing Git in that early would make things more confusing and painful for beginners who just want to start Vibe Coding. There's already a lot of basic stuff to wrap your head around, and if you add Git on top of that, you'd probably give up halfway, right? Git has its own concepts to learn (even if the AI is the one running the commands).

But you need to know that in real development, Git is a must. Especially if you want to ship an actual product, Git is your most important safety net, because you can never be sure the AI will always make the right changes.

That's why, given how I planned the earlier posts, I introduced /rewind first instead. It lets you roll back to the previous state.

But don't forget its limit:

It can only roll back changes made by the file editing tools. Changes made through Bash commands aren't covered.

Mistake #4: Expecting one sentence to build Facebook

If that's how you think about Vibe Coding, you're basically this meme:

This is probably the most common misunderstanding among beginners: thinking one Prompt to the AI is enough, like:

Build me a Facebook

Or:

Build me an expense tracker app. It should track expenses, have stats, have charts, support export, and look good.

Sure, the AI might actually pull it off. Flip on Auto Mode, run claude --permission-mode bypassPermissions, and it might just get it all done in one shot.

But... how are you going to check it?

If you can't check a product, how are you going to maintain it? When something breaks, where do you even start looking? And how do you know what it built is what you actually had in mind? Not to mention actually shipping it.

So the hands-on posts coming up will walk you through this, so your Vibe Coding product is something that "can be checked".

Mistake #5: Never checking the result when it's done

I have to say this one's a big one. From what I've seen teaching so far, a lot of people's AI habit looks like this:

> Claude Code: I've completed your request.

(User closes the window)

Yep, a lot of people really do this. They close it without even looking, and a few days later when they actually go to use it, they find the button or feature is broken, or the new feature broke an old one.

All of that comes from skipping the check. And by checking, I don't just mean glancing at the code or the screen. You need to actually use it yourself once and make sure it really does what you need.

Later posts will also cover some ways to automate checking so you don't have to click through everything by hand every time. But at least early on, walking through it yourself once is a must.

Week 1 hands-on checklist

With the mistakes out of the way, here's a hands-on checklist for week one. Go through it line by line and see whether you've actually done each one:

  • Thought through the Day 2 exercise: listed three or four visible acceptance criteria for "add an expense" (Day 2)
  • Installed Claude Code, and both claude --version and claude doctor show up fine (Day 3)
  • Created the claude-playground folder, started claude inside it, saw the welcome screen, and got /help to open (Day 3)
  • Ran the vague "make this page look better" Prompt and felt what "impossible to check" means (Day 4)
  • Used /rewind (or pressed Esc twice) to pull back the changes from that vague Prompt (Day 4)
  • Ran the small, checkable task of a random-background-color button, and understood the diff and the difference between the three options (Day 4)
  • Switched permission modes with Shift+Tab and had it hand you a plan once in Plan Mode (Day 5)
  • Sent the first plan back and confirmed the "things it won't do" actually showed up in the second plan (Day 5)
  • Looked at table usage with /context, ran the /compact and /clear experiment, and know the difference between the two (Day 6)

Wrap up

Last but not least, let's recap:

  • Glance at the diff before hitting Yes. Don't blindly agree.
  • One task, one conversation. Don't chat from morning to night.
  • Git is the real safety net. /rewind only saves you halfway.
  • Break big goals into small steps. Don't expect one sentence to build Facebook.
  • Checking the result is always your job. The AI saying it's done doesn't mean it's done.

And that's a wrap on week one.

See you tomorrow.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 6: Context and Tokens — Why AI Gets Dumber the Longer You Chat
entry.content:
Intro

Once you start using AI to actually get things done, weird stuff starts happening. You clearly gave it some rules, but it seems to forget them, answers something you didn't ask, or even changes something it already fixed back to the broken version.

Most people's first instinct when this happens is...

"Did the AI just get dumber?" "Is the AI company secretly turning down the model's IQ?"

But a lot of the time, the real problem is that the Context inside the Context Window is full, and the AI can't work properly anymore.

And you can't really talk about Context without talking about Tokens, since the two are tightly connected.

Once you get this, you'll understand why AI gets dumber the longer you chat, and why people who use AI a lot keep telling you to open a new conversation for each task.

Tokens: the building blocks of the AI world

Before we get to Context, let's meet the most important thing in the AI world: the Token. It's also the unit AI companies bill you in.

After the last few days of hands-on work, you're probably used to the "send a Prompt => AI replies" loop by now. But have you ever wondered how the AI actually "reads" what you type?

AI doesn't read word by word like we do. It first chops your text into small chunks and then does its math on those chunks. Each chunk is called a Token.

Think of Tokens as LEGO bricks. Whatever you send the AI gets broken down into individual little bricks. Once the AI has the bricks, it thinks about which bricks you probably want to come next, then snaps them together one by one and hands them back to you.

Say you send the AI this:

Hello there!

The AI would break it into something like:

  • "Hello"
  • " there"
  • "!" — three bricks

Then, based on those three bricks, it predicts which bricks you probably want next.

Different models may split Tokens differently, but they generally split by word or piece of a word.

You can also picture the AI sitting on a huge pile of bricks that are sorted into bins, like...

  • A bin for everyday conversation bricks
  • A bin for code bricks
  • A bin for bricks related to all kinds of file formats

And so on. It compares everything in those bins against the bricks you handed it. That comparing process is what we call "compute". Once it's done comparing, it snaps the result into new bricks and hands them back to you.

So for this section, just remember two things:

  • The more text you send, the more Tokens there are, and the more compute the AI has to burn.
  • It's not only your text that counts. Every word the AI replies with is a Token too.

Remember how I said at the start that "Tokens are also the billing unit"? That means every back-and-forth with the AI burns Tokens, and AI companies charge you based on how many you use.

That's also why beginners are generally told not to jump straight into pay-as-you-go API billing. You have no real sense of how many Tokens you'll burn, and one slip and your bill explodes (time to sell a kidney). For most people, a subscription plan is more than enough.

So what do Tokens have to do with AI getting dumber over time? Hang on, that's where our next main character comes in: the Context Window.

Context Window: a table with a size limit

Now that we've covered Tokens, let's meet the Context Window. In short, it's the total limit on everything the AI can "see" at once.

That's probably a bit abstract, so let me use a table as an example.

Say the Context Window is a table, and it's a 100 x 100 cm table (like the 100k Tokens Claude Code labels). Every sentence you say to the AI, every file it reads in, every command output, all of that is stuff sitting on the tabletop.

Whenever you talk to the AI, it first looks over everything on the table and then replies. It's like chatting with a friend, except this friend, after hearing your question, glances over the table, figures out what you want and how to answer, writes the answer down on a sheet of paper, puts that sheet on the table, and only then replies to you.

"Why does the AI write it on paper and put it back on the table?"

Just picture the AI as a friend with a really bad memory. If it doesn't write down what it's about to say, it forgets what it was going to say and starts making stuff up.

As you ask more and more questions, the table obviously gets more and more crowded. And then you hit a problem...

There's almost no room left on the table for anything new!

When the table is about to run out of space, the AI takes it upon itself to tidy up. While doing that, it picks out what it thinks is important, condenses it into a cheat sheet, and throws the rest away. That process is called "Auto compact".

And you have zero control over Auto compact. You can't know what it'll throw away and what it'll keep. That's exactly why the AI seems to forget rules you gave it, answer something you didn't ask, or undo things it already fixed.

So if you want to get along with AI long term, learning to manage this table is part of your daily routine (kind of like opening a million Chrome tabs and never closing any). I'll show you how to manage it later on.

The truth behind "the longer you chat, the dumber it gets"

Once you understand Tokens and the Context Window, you'll see that "the AI gets dumber over time" isn't mysterious at all.

Picture this: you've been chatting with the AI all afternoon. What does your table (the Context Window) look like? It's covered in all the notes the AI wrote down after each of your Prompts, like:

  • Your conversation history with the AI
  • File contents the AI read in
  • Output from commands the AI ran

So when the table is almost full, every AI Agent does the same thing: it helpfully condenses the earlier conversation into a summary and throws the rest away to make room for new stuff. And that compression is "lossy", meaning details get lost.

Say the rule you gave the AI at the very beginning was:

Please reply to me in Traditional Chinese.

When the AI starts clearing the table (compressing the conversation), it may decide this isn't a big deal and drop the rule during compression. And from then on, it starts replying in English.

/context: see how messy your table is right now

Now let's look at a real example. Grab the sample files from GitHub #day-6, go into claude-playground, start Claude Code, and type /context in the input box. This command shows you how much of your table is taken up right now, like...

  • How much the System Prompt takes
  • How much System Tools take
  • How much Skills take

The Context you see on your machine may look different from my screenshot above. Everyone's conversation is different, and so are the Skills and tools loaded by default, so there'll be some variation.

Early on, I'd recommend getting into the habit of checking context, because seeing how full the table is with your own eyes is way more convincing than any article. Here's what it looks like right after starting up, before doing anything:

Next, let's run a little experiment so you can watch Context fill up:

Read index.html, then explain line by line what each part of the code does. Then give me five suggestions for improving this page, and finally paste the full improved code right here in the chat for me to see. Don't touch any files yet.

This Prompt makes the AI do three table-hogging things in one go: read the whole index.html (file contents land on the table), output a long line-by-line explanation (every word it replies with is a Token), and then paste the whole file back to you again (another big stack of paper on the table).

Once it's done replying, type /context again, and you'll see the table now looks like this:

You can see it jumped from 29.3k to 49.5k, and messages went from one block to five. That's what your table looks like after chatting with the AI for a while.

/clear vs /compact: a new table vs tidying the table

After reading all that, you're probably thinking:

"If I don't want Auto compact to kick in, is there another way to deal with this?"

There is. So here are two commands you really need to know when building with AI: /clear and /compact.

First up is /clear (or /new). The idea is simple: throw everything on the table away and start over.

I say "throw everything away," but a later post will cover how to get the AI back to its original table setup every time you clear.

/compact is pretty similar to Auto compact, except you can add instructions about "what to keep". What does that mean? Basically, with Auto compact the AI decides on its own what's important. With /compact, you get to say what's important. For example, the AI might think "please reply in Traditional Chinese" doesn't matter, but with /compact you can tell it that's a key point it can't drop, so it keeps it when tidying the table.

Using it is really simple:

/compact Keep the requirements for the current feature and any unresolved issues, everything else can go

That way, when the AI compresses, it knows exactly what matters and what can be tossed.

I do want to point out that /compact isn't magic. In practice, I'd recommend running /compact when Context is around 60–70% full. Tidying up takes table space too, so if you wait until Context is at 90% before tidying, there's a good chance you'll lose something you consider important.

Both commands have their own timing and use cases, so here's a chart for reference:

flowchart TD
    A{"Table's almost full. Where's the current task at?"} -->|"Already done"| B["/clear: get a new table"]
    A -->|"Halfway, can't lose the context"| C["/compact: tidy the table<br>Add instructions for what to keep"]
    B --> D["CLAUDE.md and memory<br>come back to the new table automatically"]
    C --> E["Frees up space, keep going on the same task"]

So my personal rule of thumb is:

  • Once a task is done, get a new table (/clear).
  • If the Context Window hits around 60–70%, tidy the table first (/compact), then keep going on the same task.

This kind of control is pretty much enough to keep you out of the "dumber the longer you chat" trap. Combine it with using /compact at the right time, and you can hold on to the key points you care about within the same task.

Just to be clear: if the AI gets dumber because the AI company is short on compute, that's a totally different thing from a full Context Window. The point here is that a full Context Window makes the AI dumber, not a lack of compute. If you want to track whether AI models are actually getting dumber, check out my earlier post Is AI Getting Quietly Dumber? AIStupidLevel: A 24-Hour Watchdog for LLM Degradation. It might help.

Try watching the Context Window change

Let's go back to claude-playground for a small experiment.

If the conversation from the /context section is still open, just keep using it. If you already closed it, restart Claude Code and type this again:

Read index.html, then explain line by line what each part of the code does. Then give me five suggestions for improving this page, and finally paste the full improved code right here in the chat for me to see. Don't touch any files yet.

Let the table fill up as much as possible first (feel free to run /context to see how full it is), then move on.

Once you're ready, follow these steps and watch how the Context Window changes:

  1. Type /compact Only keep the current page's features and what's still unfinished
  2. Type /context again and compare: did the table usage go down?
  3. Ask it "What were the five improvement suggestions you just gave me?" and see how much it remembers
  4. Then ask "What features does the current page have?" It should be able to answer this one
  5. Type /clear, then ask "What features does the current page have?" again

Step 3 lets you see for yourself that compression is "lossy". In /compact we only told it to keep the features and unfinished work, not those five suggestions, so it'll likely miss some or give an incomplete answer.

Steps 4 and 5 are the same question asked twice. Before /clear, it can answer, because that's exactly the key point we told it to keep. After /clear, it can't even answer that one and has to re-read the file, because the table has been wiped.

It's possible it still answers correctly, because the AI has an Auto Memory feature that decides on its own what's important and saves it automatically.

Wrap up

Quick recap of the key points:

  • Tokens are like LEGO bricks, and the Context Window is a table with a size limit, covered with your conversation with the AI, the files it read, command outputs, and so on.
  • The AI getting dumber over time isn't necessarily about lack of compute or the model getting worse. The table may just be too full, and the important stuff got compressed and diluted.
  • /context to look at the table, /clear to clear it, /compact to tidy it.
  • Core rule of thumb: one task, one conversation, and use /compact [what to keep] to hold on to the key points.

That's about it for today. See you tomorrow.
