entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 5: Permissions and Plan Mode — Stop Hitting Yes on Everything
entry.content:
Intro

After yesterday's first little exercise, the AI probably asked you a few questions, and at least once it asked "Can I change this?" — and you decided whether to hit "Yes" and let it edit the file.

But... use it long enough and you'll notice those confirmation prompts show up a lot. Then human nature kicks in, you start hitting Yes on autopilot, all the way to the end, and then it hits you: "Oh no, I just broke the whole project!"

So today I want to properly explain this "Permission" mechanism — which actions it'll ask you about and which ones it won't — so you can avoid getting nagged to death while still keeping your project safe from random edits.

The AI's access control

Remember this screenshot from yesterday?

Notice that even though we were the ones who asked the AI to open the browser, it still asked: "Is it OK if I open the browser?"

Weird, right? We literally sent this prompt ourselves:

Please open index.html for me. I want to see the result in my browser.

So why is it still asking? That's what this chapter is about: the "Permission" mechanism.

This isn't unique to Claude Code — other AI Agent tools have something similar. It decides which actions are allowed and which ones need your confirmation first, and it's not random.

How permissions basically work

The core idea is actually pretty simple. It comes down to whether an action leaves a mark on your computer. There are basically two kinds of actions:

  • Actions that leave a mark (a trace)
  • Actions that don't leave a mark

What does that mean? Imagine that before doing anything, the AI asks itself one question:

"If I do this, will it leave a mark on this computer? If so, I need to stop and ask the user whether that's OK."

On the flip side, if it's just looking at / reading files or searching, it mostly won't ask you.

But! Editing files, creating new files, that kind of thing — anything that leaves a mark on your computer — by default it'll stop and let you know what it's about to do.

OK, I know that might sound a bit wordy, so just remember this one line:

Looking doesn't need permission. Touching does.

Once you get this big-picture idea of access control, you'll see that the AI asking isn't it being annoying. It's doing something that might leave a mark on your computer, so it stops to ask you:

"Can I do this?"

One thing to watch out for: just because a command didn't trigger a permission prompt once doesn't mean it'll never ask, and it doesn't mean it's guaranteed to be safe either. That mostly depends on your current mode and the rules you've approved before.

The six permission modes

Now that you've got the basic idea of access control, let's go a bit deeper into permission modes.

First, a quick experiment. Just like yesterday, go into the claude-playground folder and launch Claude Code. Then press Shift+Tab a few times. You'll see the mode near the input box cycle through these:

  1. manual mode on
  2. accept edits on
  3. plan mode on
  4. auto mode on (not everyone has this one — I'll explain in a sec)

These are the permission modes you'll use day to day. (Remember to switch back to manual mode on.)

Here's a fun little detail: if you go dig through the official docs (Permission modes (official docs)), you'll notice the names don't quite match what's on your screen. For example, the docs' default mode is actually what shows up as manual mode on. So I've matched them up for you below:

On-screen labelName in the docsBehavior
manual mode ondefaultAsks every time before touching anything
accept edits onacceptEditsCommon file edits and filesystem commands go through automatically; everything else still asks
plan mode onplanResearch mode: it researches first, then asks whether you'll let it run the plan
auto mode onautoBasically allows everything, but with some safety checks running behind the scenes, so it asks way less often

I want to call out accept edits on (acceptEdits) specifically. In this mode, common file edits and filesystem commands get auto-approved, for example:

  • Creating folders (mkdir)
  • Moving things (mv)
  • Deleting things (rm)

Commands like these become approved by default, so it doesn't ask "Is this OK?" every time. But you should still get in the habit of checking what the AI is about to do, because I've personally had an AI move my entire project folder somewhere else, and for a while I couldn't find anything.

Now a bit about the official docs. They list six permission modes in total. On top of the four above, there are two more:

  • dontAsk: In this mode, anything that would normally trigger a permission prompt just gets denied. It only runs actions you've pre-approved. This is great for automation scripts (where a program runs the AI Agent by itself), which is why it doesn't show up in the Shift+Tab cycle.
  • bypassPermissions: It doesn't ask you anything and just lets everything through. I really don't recommend using this casually. It's basically meant for sandboxes (an environment isolated from your actual computer). If you turn it on carelessly on your own machine, it's like handing over your house keys and leaving the front door wide open. It doesn't show up in the Shift+Tab cycle either — you have to add a flag to the launch command to get it.

So the extra dontAsk and bypassPermissions modes only show up when you pass a flag at launch; you can't switch to them normally. Here's how you'd launch them, just for reference (please don't use these casually):

# Launch in dontAsk mode
claude --permission-mode dontAsk
# Launch in bypassPermissions mode
claude --permission-mode bypassPermissions

If you do use bypassPermissions, make absolutely sure you're in an isolated environment (a Sandbox). Otherwise one day you'll be the main character of a disaster story on social media.

Plan Mode

I highly recommend Plan Mode — it's also the mode I personally use the most. The idea is: plan first, think first, and only then decide whether to actually do it.

With Plan Mode on, the AI becomes read-only. It can read your project and do research, but it can't change a single file.

Enough talk, let's actually try it. Remember where we left off with yesterday's practice file? You should have ended on this request:

The button text should be "Change background color", not "Click me".

If you can't find it or don't have it, you can grab the practice files from GitHub #day5.

Today we're going to use Plan Mode to add some stuff to this practice page and turn it into a simple personal profile page. The profile needs three sections added at once, which makes it perfect for practicing Plan Mode.

So launch claude to get into Claude Code, and press Shift+Tab in the input box to switch to plan mode.

Once you've confirmed it says plan mode on, copy and paste this into the input box:

I want to add three sections to index.html: an About Me section, a Skills list, and Contact info.
Keep the original heading and the "Change background color" button.

So the AI isn't working with less information than you, remember to first ask it What's in this folder? What's inside index.html?, and then send the text above. That way it knows what you actually want.

There's a pretty good chance you'll see a screen like this next:

Why is it asking these? Because the task (the prompt) we gave it has gaps, so it gives you multiple-choice questions to cut down the chances of it making changes you didn't expect.

Next, the AI will throw a big wall of information at you. This is the heart of Plan Mode: it researches your project first and then hands you a plan, and you decide whether to let it go ahead. Here's the full plan I got, for reference:

Ready to code?

Here is Claude's plan:
Add three sections to index.html

Context

day-5/claude-playground/index.html is currently only 17 lines: an <h1>, a line saying "Nothing here yet.", an external link, and a button that randomly changes the background color. It's a vibe coding practice page and doesn't have real content yet.

This change adds three sections — About Me, Skills, and Contact — while keeping the original heading and the background color button. The content will use neutral placeholder text (no made-up personal details) for Ray to replace later. It'll also add a small bit of inline CSS so the page stays readable with three more sections.

Stick with the current single-file style: no external fonts, no dark mode, no splitting into multiple files.

Files to change

Just one: day-5/claude-playground/index.html

Approach

1. What stays untouched

- <h1>Hello，這是我的 Vibe Coding 練習頁</h1> — text unchanged
- The button <button type="button" id="bgBtn">隨機換背景色</button> and the <script> at the bottom — completely untouched, including id="bgBtn"

2. Two things that will change (please confirm when approving)

- Line 8, "Nothing here yet.": this won't be true once the three sections are added, so I suggest replacing it with a short intro line (placeholder text). If you'd like to keep it, just say so.
- Line 9, the israynotarray.com link: I suggest moving it into the Contact section so it's not stuck awkwardly between the heading and the sections. The link itself and target="_blank" stay, and I'll add rel="noopener noreferrer" while I'm at it.

3. New structure

Below the heading and above the button, add a <main> containing three <section>s, each starting with an <h2>:

┌──────────┬───────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Section  │ Markup                │ Sample content                                               │
├──────────┼───────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ About Me │ <h2> + one or two <p> │ A neutral line like "I'm OOO, and I mainly do frontend..."   │
├──────────┼───────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Skills   │ <h2> + <ul><li>       │ HTML / CSS / JavaScript / Git, etc., each with a short note  │
├──────────┼───────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Contact  │ <h2> + <ul><li>       │ Email (mailto: placeholder), blog link, one other social     │
└──────────┴───────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Put a short HTML comment saying "edit here" next to each placeholder value so it's easy to replace later.

Also add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> to the <head> — once there's a max-width on the layout, phones will zoom it out without this line.

4. CSS scope

One inline <style> block in the <head>, doing only four things:

- body: system font stack, line-height: 1.7, max-width around 40rem centered, padding
- section: vertical spacing between sections
- ul: spacing between list items
- button: a bit of padding and cursor: pointer

Key constraint: don't set a background on anything other than body. The button's JS writes the color into document.body.style.backgroundColor (an inline style), so as long as section / main don't have their own background, the color change will still show through the whole page. body itself can have a default background; the inline style has higher priority, so they won't conflict.

Not adding: external fonts, dark mode, favicon, animations, CSS variables.

Verification

1. Open day-5/claude-playground/index.html directly in the browser
2. Confirm all three sections are there, the heading text wasn't changed, and the layout is readable on both desktop and narrow windows
3. Click "Random background color" a few times — the whole page background should change, with no white blocks from the sections covering it
4. Open the DevTools Console and confirm there are no errors (getElementById('bgBtn') must not become null)

Once the plan is out, you'll see some options below it:

  • Yes, and use auto mode (approve it and switch to auto mode)
  • Yes, manually approve edits (approve it and switch to manual mode)
  • Tell Claude what to change (don't approve it; tell Claude Code what to change)

The wording may differ slightly depending on your version — as long as the meaning matches, you're fine. But for now, don't pick Yes, and use auto mode. Press Esc to leave the menu instead, since we're just getting a feel for how Plan Mode works.

With that done, let's go over a few key points about Plan Mode. When you're in Plan Mode, I strongly recommend actually reading the plan. Things like:

  • Which files is it planning to touch or change? (Does it go beyond what you expected?)
  • Does the order of the steps make sense?

If you're worried you won't understand what the AI is saying (tons of technical jargon, for example), you can use "Tell Claude what to change" to ask it to explain things more simply. That's one of the handy tricks for actually understanding what it's about to do.

That way you won't end up with that "I have no idea what it just did" feeling. The whole point of this mode is to let you see the plan first, then decide whether to go ahead.

A controlled failure: revise the Plan Mode plan

Now that you know the basics, let's try the other key part of Plan Mode: revising the plan.

Right now we've pressed Esc, left the menu, and we're back at the input box. But the plan we just got is still sitting there in the conversation.

Let's try revising it. Copy and paste this into the input box:

Don't run this plan yet. Revise it and give it to me again:

1. Don't include email in the contact info. Use GitHub and Threads links instead.
2. Only change index.html. Don't add any packages or other files.
3. Make my name a link to "https://israynotarray.com/" with target="_blank".

Also, list "What I won't do" at the very top of the new plan.

You'll get another big chunk of plan back:

Ready to code?

Here is Claude's plan:

Add three sections to index.html (revised)

What I won't do

- No new files: no style.css, script.js, or README, and no touching day-4 or any other folder
- No packages: no npm, no build tools, no package.json
- No external resources: no Google Fonts, no CDN, no favicon, no images
- No email: contact info only has GitHub and Threads links, no mailto:
- No touching the button or its JS: id="bgBtn" and the background color <script> stay exactly as they are
- No changes to the <h1> heading text
- No extra design: no dark mode, CSS variables, animations, or responsive breakpoints

Context

day-5/claude-playground/index.html is currently 17 lines: an <h1>, a line saying "Nothing here yet.", an external link, and a button that randomly changes the background color.

This change adds three sections — About Me, Skills, and Contact — while keeping the original heading and button. The content uses neutral placeholder text (no made-up personal details) to be replaced later, plus a small bit of inline CSS to keep the layout readable. All changes stay within the same file.

Files to change

day-5/claude-playground/index.html — only this one.

Approach
1. What stays untouched

- <h1>Hello，這是我的 Vibe Coding 練習頁</h1>
- <button type="button" id="bgBtn">隨機換背景色</button> and the entire <script> at the bottom

2. Two changes

- Line 8, "Nothing here yet.": this won't be true once the three sections are in, so replace it with a short intro line (placeholder text). If you'd like to keep it, just say so.
- Line 9, the standalone israynotarray.com link: remove it. Its job is taken over by the name link in the About Me section below, so the same URL doesn't show up twice on the page.

3. Three sections

Below the heading and above the button, add a <main> containing three <section>s, each starting with an <h2>:

About Me — <h2> + one or two <p>. The name should be a link:

<p>I'm <a href="https://israynotarray.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">是 Ray 不是 Array</a>, and I mainly do frontend development...</p>

You can change the display text to whatever name you want later; the href stays fixed at https://israynotarray.com/. rel="noopener noreferrer" is the standard security practice to pair with target="_blank", so I'm adding it while I'm at it.

Skills — <h2> + <ul><li>, listing HTML / CSS / JavaScript / Git, etc., each with a short note.

Contact — <h2> + <ul><li>, two items:

┌─────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Item    │ href                                      │ Notes                                                               │
├─────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ GitHub  │ https://github.com/hsiangfeng             │ Guessed from this repo's git user — please double-check; edit if off │
├─────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Threads │ https://www.threads.net/@ + placeholder   │ I don't know the account, so I'm leaving a placeholder with a TODO  │
└─────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Both get target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer".

Put a short HTML comment saying "edit here" next to each placeholder value.

Also add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> to the <head> — once there's a width limit, phones will zoom it out without this line.

4. CSS scope

One inline <style> block in the <head>, doing only four things:

- body: system font stack, line-height: 1.7, max-width around 40rem centered, padding
- section: vertical spacing between sections
- ul: spacing between items
- button: padding and cursor: pointer

Key constraint: no element other than body gets a background. The button's JS writes the color into document.body.style.backgroundColor (an inline style), so as long as main / section don't have their own background, the color change will still show through the whole page.

Verification

1. Open day-5/claude-playground/index.html directly in the browser
2. All three sections are there, the <h1> text is unchanged, and it's readable on both desktop and narrow windows
3. Click "Random background color" a few times — the whole page background changes, with no white blocks from the sections covering it
4. All three links (name, GitHub, Threads) open in a new tab and point to the right URLs
5. No errors in the DevTools Console (getElementById('bgBtn') must not be null)
6. git status should show only index.html as modified

This time, the plan clearly includes a few things:

  • What it won't do: no email, no new packages, only one file touched
  • What it will do: three sections, keep the original heading and button, and the button still works

If anything's missing or there's something extra, you can use "Tell Claude what to change" to ask for revisions, and keep sending it back until it matches exactly what you want. That process is basically forcing you to build the habit of "read the plan first, then act".

Once the plan is revised to your satisfaction, this is when you can actually hit "Yes, manually approve edits".

Notice I said "Yes, manually approve edits", not "Yes, and use auto mode". That's because I want every step the AI takes to pass in front of your eyes, so it doesn't do something you didn't want. Once you approve, it leaves Plan Mode and gets to work.

When it's done, don't forget to verify the result. For example:

  • No weird extra files showed up.
  • Open it in the browser and check that the three sections and the two social links are all there.
  • Click the "Change background color" button and make sure the original feature still works.

That last one is especially important. After the AI adds or changes a feature, we have to make sure the old features weren't broken — and this is a good chance to start building that habit.

Personally, I mostly reach for Plan Mode when a change touches multiple files (roughly two or more), when I'm working on a project I'm not familiar with, or when I have no idea how to approach something. It also saves quite a bit on cost (we'll cover Tokens in a later chapter).

Here's that decision flow as a diagram:

flowchart TD
    A{"Touching two or more files, unfamiliar project,<br>or you don't have a plan yet?"} -->|"Yes"| B["Switch to plan mode on<br>Read the plan, send it back if you're not happy"]
    B --> C["Once the plan looks good, pick<br>Yes, manually approve edits"]
    A -->|"No"| D["Stay in manual mode on<br>Get started, confirm each step yourself"]
    C --> D

Wrapping up

As usual, let's sum up today's key points:

  • The basic access control idea comes down to "looking doesn't need permission, touching does".
  • The core modes you'll use:
    • manual mode on (default): asks every time before doing anything
    • accept edits on (acceptEdits): common file edits and filesystem commands go through automatically; everything else still asks
    • plan mode on (plan): researches first, then asks whether you'll let it run the plan
    • auto mode on (auto): allows everything, but with safety checks running behind the scenes
  • Use Shift+Tab to switch modes
  • If you don't like the plan, send it back. Planning things out before doing them works a lot better.

Hopefully this gave you a better understanding of Permissions and Plan Mode.

If that all makes sense, see you tomorrow.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 4: Your First Task — The Smallest Loop for Changing Code
entry.content:
Intro

If you've made it to this chapter, I'm going to assume you've already got Claude Code installed, because today we're finally getting our hands a little dirty.

The goal today is small, though. We're going to use a tiny practice file to run through one full loop of "ask it to do something → see what it did → decide whether to keep it → pull it back if you change your mind".

Don't underestimate this loop. Once we start building the expense tracker app later in the series, pretty much everything revolves around this exact flow and mindset.

Create your first practice file

Before we start, let's warm up a bit. Open your terminal and either drag the claude-playground project folder into it, or just cd into it:

cd claude-playground

Then copy and paste the command below to quickly create your first index.html practice file:

echo '<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="zh-Hant">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>我的練習頁（是 Ray 不是 Array）</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello，這是我的 Vibe Coding 練習頁</h1>
  <p>目前這裡什麼都還沒有。</p>
  <a href="https://israynotarray.com/" target="_blank">是 Ray 不是 Array</a>
</body></html>' > index.html

The content is really simple — just a basic heading, a line of text, and a link. The simpler the file, the more you can focus on how Claude Code behaves, instead of getting distracted by complicated code.

If creating the file doesn't go smoothly, you can grab the full example files here: https://github.com/hsiangfeng/ithelp-2026-vibe-coding. Just click "Code → Download ZIP" and you'll have the practice files.

Ask questions before you change anything

Once that's ready, type claude in the terminal to launch Claude Code. Before you do, double-check that you're actually inside the claude-playground directory, otherwise you might run into some weird problems.

Also, your permission mode should be the default "manual mode on" (which the official docs call default). That means every time it wants to touch your files, it'll stop and ask you first. We'll get into the details on Day 5.

So we're not going to ask the AI to change anything right away. Instead, we'll first have it confirm "what it can see and what it understands right now", like this:

What's in this folder? What's inside index.html?

A lot of people get curious at this point: "Why bother?"

There are actually two reasons:

  1. To confirm Claude Code sees the same files you do. This also catches cases where you didn't actually end up in the claude-playground directory, or the file didn't save, or got saved in the wrong place.
  2. To let Claude Code understand the current state first, so it doesn't misread whatever you type next and make changes you didn't expect.

As long as your result looks similar to (or the same as) mine, you're in the same spot I am, and you can keep going.

Of course, even if you don't ask "What's in this folder? What's inside index.html?", it'll go read the files on its own anyway. It's just a personal habit of mine to check what it can see first — it avoids a lot of unnecessary misunderstandings.

A controlled failure: give it a vague prompt on purpose

I'm not going to start by showing you the "right answer". I think you should experience the wrong way firsthand, because that's how you'll actually understand why the right way is better.

So copy and paste this into Claude Code's input box:

Make this page look better. You decide how.

Don't be scared! Go ahead and send it. It's just a practice file, and every time Claude Code receives a prompt, it automatically saves a restore point (this mechanism is called a checkpoint). Even if things go sideways, you can get it back.

A line like "Make this page look better. You decide how." is what we call a prompt (as in "writing a prompt"). Anything you send can be called a prompt — it's basically the thing you want Claude Code to do. Definitely remember this one.

Along the way it may ask you some permission questions. That red-and-green chunk in the middle of the window is the change it's planning to make (red is what it wants to delete, green is what it wants to add — I'll teach you how to read it properly in a bit). For now, just glance at it so it looks familiar. Then you'll see three options:

  • Yes
  • Yes, allow all edits during this session (shift+tab)
  • No

Pick "Yes" here, which means you're approving this one change, and it'll start editing the file. (Please don't pick "Yes, allow all edits during this session (shift+tab)" — that option auto-approves every edit after this one, which is really not safe for beginners.)

Then Claude Code will tell you what it changed and what it did:

So how do you actually look at the result? Easy, just tell it:

Please open index.html for me. I want to see the result in my browser.

If a permission prompt like the one below pops up, no need to worry — just allow it:

You should now see something like this, and it'll probably look a bit different for everyone:

Pretty interesting, right? The same prompt can produce all kinds of different results. That's AI randomness, and that randomness is exactly why you can't predict what it's going to turn the page into — which leads to the problem of "you can't verify it".

You might actually think the design looks pretty nice and wonder, "So where's the failure?"

Try answering these three questions:

  1. What exactly did it change, in total?
  2. Why did it change it to this, and not something else?
  3. Does this count as "done right"? What's your standard for judging that?

A bit hard to answer, isn't it? Exactly. That's the first big takeaway: "you can't control it". Just like we saw, the same sentence — "Make this page look better. You decide how." — can give completely different results for different people, different models, or even the same person sending it twice.

Because you didn't define any acceptance criteria or tell it what style you wanted, the AI has no choice but to fill in the blank called "looks better" with its own imagination. And you have no way to tell whether it got it right or wrong. That's why sending the exact same sentence again might give you something totally different.

So whether the page looks nice is secondary. The real problem is that you've lost the ability to verify. You can't say whether this result is right or wrong — only whether you like it or not.

If you're just building a toy for yourself, that's fine. But if you want to build something people can actually use, "can't verify it" becomes a serious problem, because you have no idea how far you are from the goal, or what the next step should be.

Pull it back with /rewind

Now that we've been through that first task, let's undo the failure. This is where the checkpoint mechanism I mentioned earlier comes in.

Type /rewind in the input box, or press Esc twice while the input box is empty — that also brings up the restore menu. You should see your conversation history. Find the "Make this page look better. You decide how." line and select it.

The menu first lists the prompts you've sent in this conversation. Pick which one you want to go back to (here, the "Make this page look better. You decide how." one), and then you should see these choices:

  1. Restore code and conversation
  2. Restore conversation (only the conversation; your code stays as-is)
  3. Restore code (only the code; the conversation stays as-is)
  4. Summarize from here (compress the conversation from this point on into a summary)
  5. Summarize up to here (compress everything before this point into a summary)
  6. Never mind

Pick "Restore code and conversation". That puts both the code and the conversation back to how they were before you sent that vague prompt, and the prompt itself will be waiting in the input box so you can quickly edit it.

Heads up: /rewind only restores changes made with Claude Code's editing tools. If anything got deleted or moved with a Bash command along the way, that can't be restored. That's why real projects almost always pair this with Git (a tool that saves every version of your files — we'll formally introduce it in a later chapter), which is much safer.

By now you've probably noticed that "wander off, then pull it back" is a big deal, and it's actually one of the key skills in Vibe Coding. Going off track isn't the problem. Not being able to get back is.

Give it a small task you can verify

Next, I'll show you a small task that can be verified (and I mean really small). Delete the "Make this page look better. You decide how." text in the input box and replace it with this:

Add a button to the page. When I click it, the whole page's background color changes to a random color.

Quick tip: pressing Ctrl + C in the input box clears the whole thing instantly, so you don't have to delete it character by character. Just be careful — if you press it while the AI is still thinking, it'll interrupt it. So wait until it's done replying first.

You might be thinking, "How is this verifiable?" It actually is:

  • Is there a button on the page? You can tell at a glance.
  • Does the background change color when you click it? One click and you know.

Right or wrong, there's no gray area.

As for what the button looks like, where it goes, or what color it is — we let the AI decide, because those aren't what we're checking this time. What matters is "is there a button, and does clicking it change the color?" That's what a verifiable small task looks like.

After you send it, don't rush to look at the result. Read its reply first. Usually it'll tell you what it changed and which tools it used, and then ask whether you want to open the browser to see the result.

Read, Edit, and Bash are Claude Code's built-in tools, and they're the three beginners see the most: reading files, editing files, and running commands. It decides on its own which tools to use for each task. For now, just recognizing these three is enough.

In theory, your browser should open at this point. If it doesn't, you can tell the AI:

Please open index.html for me. I want to see the result in my browser.

Congrats — you've just described a minimal task that "can be verified".

Reading the diff: red is deleted, green is added

All that red and green from earlier actually has a proper name: it's called a diff, meaning "difference" — the difference between the code before and after a change.

This is your most important tool for tracking what Claude Code did, and it's also what you base your decision on when choosing whether to accept a change.

Remember this:

  • Red lines are what it wants to delete (usually starting with -)
  • Green lines are what it wants to add (usually starting with +)

Build this habit: at least glance at what it touched and check whether it matches what you expected before you hit Yes.

Below that, there are basically three options:

OptionWhat it meansWhen to use it
YesApprove this one time onlyUse this one for pretty much everything early on
Yes, allow all edits during this sessionAuto-approve every edit for the rest of this conversationWhen you already trust where this task is heading
No, and tell Claude what to do differentlyReject it and tell it what to changeWhen the direction's off or you want a different approach

The exact wording may differ slightly depending on your version, so go by what's on your screen.

The third option deserves a bit more explanation. It's not just a cancel button — you can follow it up with a sentence that steers it back on track. For example, "The button text should be 'Change background color', not 'Click me'":

The button text should be "Change background color", not "Click me".

It'll redo the change and show you a new diff to confirm.

I won't walk through the third option in detail here — give it a try yourself.

Wrapping up

Let's recap today's minimal loop. This diagram should make the whole flow clearer:

flowchart TD
    A["You give an instruction"] --> B["Claude reads files and analyzes"]
    B --> C["Proposes a change: shows you the diff"]
    C --> D{"You review"}
    D -->|"Yes"| E["Change applied"]
    D -->|"No: tell it what to change"| B
    E --> F["You verify the result"]
    F -->|"OK"| G["Done, move to the next task"]
    F -->|"Something's off"| H["/rewind to restore"]
    H --> A

  • Ask before you change: asking questions is zero risk. Let it understand the current state, and make sure it didn't get the wrong idea.
  • Give it specific, small tasks, and watch its tool messages along the way so you know what it touched.
  • At least glance at the diff before hitting Yes. If the direction's wrong, use the third option to steer it straight.
  • If you regret something, use /rewind (or press Esc twice). Just remember it can't undo changes made through Bash.
  • We deliberately let a vague prompt fail once. The failure wasn't that the page looked ugly — it was that you "couldn't say whether it was right or wrong". Then we used "restore → rewrite the request → verify again" to pull things back on track.

That's it for this one. See you tomorrow.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 3: Installing Claude Code and Picking a Subscription Plan
entry.content:
Intro

Now that the basic concepts and the series intro are out of the way, it's time to get our AI Agent — Claude Code — installed on your computer.

This part is really simple — one command and you're done. But from teaching this in person, I've found that a lot of people get stuck for ages on "which plan do I actually need? How much do I have to spend to get started?" So in this post I'll explain the subscription plans first, then walk you through installing Claude Code, logging in, and making sure it works.

By the end of today, your computer will have its very own on-call errand runner intern.

Does Vibe Coding cost money?

This is probably the question people ask the most, so let me just give you the answer:

Yes. Absolutely.

I'll be honest: paying for an AI subscription is really the cleanest, least-hassle option, and it saves you from wasting a lot of time figuring out the limits of free plans.

On top of that, Claude Code itself isn't free. A free Claude account doesn't include Claude Code. You either subscribe to the Pro or Max plan, or go the API route and pay by usage (I'll explain in a bit why I don't recommend the latter).

So either way, if you want to Vibe Code something into existence, you're just going to have to accept it and pull out that magic little card.

That doesn't mean you should swipe blindly, though, so below I've laid out what each plan is for and who it fits, so you can pick based on your own needs.

So which plan should you choose? Here's a quick table for reference (just a reminder: the official pricing page is always the most accurate):

PlanWhat it isWho it's for
ProEntry-level personal subscription; use web Claude and Claude Code togetherIndividuals starting out with Vibe Coding — like you, following this series
MaxHeavy-use personal plan, with several times Pro's usagePeople who use it heavily every day and keep hitting Pro's limits. This is the plan I'm on
TeamTeam plan with multi-user managementCompanies or teams rolling it out
EnterpriseEnterprise plan with full security and admin featuresLarge organizations
API pay-as-you-goNo subscription; billed by usage with an API keyPeople with unpredictable usage who want precise control over spending

If it's your first time trying this, I'd suggest starting with the Pro plan rather than jumping straight to Max. If things are going smoothly later and you keep running into the limits, upgrading to Max then is totally fine. For subscription and upgrade pricing details, go with the official page.

This series focuses on the subscription plans. The AI isn't any smarter on Pro versus Max — the only difference is usage allowance and limits.

As for the API option, I personally don't really recommend it, because if you don't keep it under control, you might go broke.

Installing the AI Agent - Claude Code

Assuming you've already bought a subscription, the next step is obviously to install Claude Code.

Open up your Terminal, Command Prompt, or PowerShell, and paste in the install command from the official docs. There are official install methods for macOS, Linux, and Windows.

On macOS, the built-in app is called Terminal — just search for "Terminal" with Spotlight (Cmd + Space). On Windows, search for PowerShell in the Start menu.

Since I'm on macOS, I'll demo the macOS install. Just open Terminal and paste this line:

curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

Or, if you're like me and prefer Homebrew, you can use this instead:

brew install --cask claude-code

One thing to watch out for here: the Homebrew install gives you the stable version, and stable usually lags behind the latest official release. I've actually run into this myself — after a new model came out, the model list in the stable version of Claude Code didn't show it, and I had to wait for an update before I could pick it.

So if you always want the newest features and models, I'd still recommend the official curl command, or installing the latest version with brew install --cask claude-code@latest.

There's a small detail on Windows: if Git isn't installed on your computer, Claude Code will use PowerShell instead of Bash to run commands. Everything still works, but the official docs do recommend installing Git for Windows — and I'll be asking you to install Git later anyway.

Whichever install method you pick, once you've entered it, just wait for it to finish. I already have Claude Code installed, so I'm not including screenshots of the install process here.

The official docs also offer an npm install method (npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code). If the commands above keep failing, you can use it as a backup. It does require a Node.js environment, though, which might be a bit of a hassle if you're not familiar with Node.js.

Once it's installed, close your terminal and open it again so Claude Code gets loaded properly. Then run these two commands in the terminal to check that the install worked:

claude --version # Show the version number
claude doctor # Show the installation status

If you hit any errors during the install, don't panic. Try pasting the error message into claude.ai or whatever AI chat tool you normally use to help figure out the problem. For install environment issues like this, pasting the full error message usually gets you a solid direction for debugging.

Logging in to Claude Code for the first time

Once it's installed, create a folder (call it claude-playground) somewhere quick and easy to find, so you can get to it every day when you practice. Then open your terminal and drag the folder into it. You should get a path — just press Enter and the terminal will take you into that folder.

If you're more comfortable with commands, you can also run mkdir claude-playground to create the folder, then cd claude-playground to go into it. mkdir stands for make directory — it creates a folder. cd stands for change directory — it switches into a folder.

Once you're inside the folder, just type claude in the terminal:

claude # Start Claude Code

The first time you launch it, you'll see a few setup prompts:

  1. Choose the text style that looks best with your terminal: Pick whichever code style looks best to you. I personally prefer "Dark mode".
  2. Claude Code can be used with your Claude subscription or billed based on API usage through your Console account: This is asking you to choose your Claude account type. Pick "Claude account with subscription", since we'll be using Claude Code with a subscription plan.

After you choose "Claude account with subscription", a login page should pop up in your browser. Just click "Authorize" and you're logged in.

Once you've logged in successfully, you should see something like this:

Reading the welcome screen

After logging in, don't rush to start typing. Let's first make sense of that welcome screen. Here's an annotated image:

The main things to pay attention to are:

  • Text input box: This is where you interact with Claude Code. From now on, you'll give it instructions and tasks through this box.
  • Current model: Shows the name of the model you're using. Each model has its own level of smarts and speed. This series will mostly use Opus 5 (even though the screenshot shows Opus 4.8).
  • Current folder: Shows the path of the folder you launched Claude Code from.
  • Thinking level: Shows Claude Code's thinking level. The higher it is, the more carefully it thinks — and the slower it gets. The default is fine for this series, so leave it alone for now and just know what this indicator means.
  • Permission mode indicator: Near the input box you'll also see the current permission mode. The default is manual mode on (older versions might show default, or nothing at all). It decides whether Claude Code has to ask you before touching your files. I'll cover the details in Day 5 — for today, just know where to find it.

Of course, you might not see all of this the first time you launch it, since some of it needs extra setup before it shows up. Check out Claude Code Status Line Setup: Monitor Context Usage and Rate Limit in Real-Time, which walks you through how to set it up.

One more important point: when Claude Code starts, its world basically revolves around the folder you launched it from. What it can see and what it can touch is basically just the stuff inside that folder. So checking which folder you're launching from will be the first thing you do every day when you start work — and it really matters.

The first time you launch Claude Code in a new folder, it'll ask "Do you trust the files in this folder?" This is asking whether you want to let it read what's in the folder. If it's a folder you created yourself, just choose to trust it.

Your first command

Before we wrap up, try typing /help in the input box. Once you do, you should see some help text:

This is Claude Code's built-in intro, with explanations for things like !, @, and the arrow keys. Take a look when you have a minute.

Today's small challenge

I've got a little homework for you before the day ends. Try to hit all of these:

  • Run claude --version in the terminal and see a version number
  • Run claude doctor in the terminal and see the installation status displayed normally
  • Create a folder called claude-playground, go into it from the terminal, launch claude, and see the welcome screen
  • Open /help successfully (then type /exit to get back to your normal terminal)

If you really get stuck, feel free to leave a comment under this post. I'll do my best to help once I see it.

Wrap-up

So, what did we do today?

  • Picked a plan that fits you. As an individual you can start with Pro and upgrade to Max later if you really need it (if you've got more money than you know what to do with, go straight for Max 20x).
  • Installed Claude Code in your environment.
  • Logged in with your Claude account and used /help to check out Claude's intro screen.
  • Learned to read the model name, current folder, and permission mode indicator on the welcome screen.

At this point, our Claude Code environment is all set. See you tomorrow for the rest.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 2: What Is Vibe Coding? A Different Kind of Knowing
entry.content:
Intro

Today let's look at where the term "Vibe Coding" came from and what it actually means. The whole series is built on this term, so it'd feel kind of wrong not to get to know it first, right? As usual with my posts, before getting hands-on I like to understand where the background knowledge comes from.

Of course, you're also totally free to ignore the history.

But let me tell you a little secret: a lot of people imagine Vibe Coding as "lying back while AI builds everything for you". If that misunderstanding doesn't get cleared up first, over the next 28 days you might find out that Vibe Coding is nothing like what you had in mind.

Where did Vibe Coding come from?

The term Vibe Coding was coined by Andrej Karpathy. He's the former AI director at Tesla and one of the founding members of OpenAI — Tesla plus OpenAI should tell you he's a heavyweight in the AI world. In February 2025, he posted this on X:

There's a new kind of coding I call "vibe coding", where you fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists.

If you read the original, you can tell Karpathy was saying this in a half-joking, self-deprecating way: talk to the AI, paste every error message straight back to it, don't even look at the code. Great fun for a weekend project, and he said himself that this approach "mostly works".

"Mostly works" carries a bit of a caveat. It basically works, but whether it's stable, reliable, and maintainable is anyone's guess.

But nobody expected the term to outgrow its original meaning so fast. It went from a slightly self-mocking post to a catch-all term for having AI build software for you using natural language, and eventually Collins Dictionary even picked it as its 2025 Word of the Year lol.

"No coding skills needed" — is that true?

I think that statement is half true and half false, and the false half happens to be exactly what decides whether a project succeeds.

What do I mean?

  • The true part: The barrier to writing code really has dropped. Before, building a small project might take days or even weeks of learning syntax, memorizing APIs, and digging through docs. Now, as long as you can type, AI can write the code for you.
  • The false part: The ability to understand and judge hasn't gone anywhere. You no longer have to write code line by line, but you need three other skills instead: describing, verifying, and breaking things down.

These three are actually pretty common skills in everyday life — AI just amplifies them:

  • Describing: Turning the fuzzy idea in your head, "I want to build an expense tracker", into concrete requirements the AI can actually work from, instead of tossing it one vague sentence and calling it a day.
  • Verifying: After it's done, you need a way to check whether it's what you wanted and whether it broke something else along the way, instead of stopping the moment the AI says "done".
  • Breaking it down: Cutting a big goal into small steps that can each be finished in one go, where mistakes are easy to find, instead of handing over one huge goal and hoping for the best.

At this point, let me ask you something. Say you ask the AI to build a feature, and it rapidly fires off changes to a bunch of files. The screen seems to work, but deep down you have no idea whether it's actually right.

Why? Because you can't be sure about these three things:

  • What did it do?
  • Did it do it right?
  • Does the feature actually work?

And that's exactly what this series trains you on.

This is why I say Vibe Coding "isn't about not needing to know — it's a different kind of knowing". The barrier hasn't disappeared. It's shifted from your hands needing to write code to your brain needing to judge, and I'd say the learning curve for the latter is friendlier (probably?).

Three types of AI Coding tools

Now that we've got the backstory, let's get to know the kind of tool we're about to use.

There are tons of AI tools out there, but just looking at how much of the development the AI can handle for you, they fall into three types:

  • Type 1, autocomplete: You type a bit, and the AI fills in the rest for you. The best-known example is GitHub Copilot. You're completely in control here — it just makes you type a bit faster.
  • Type 2, chat Q&A: You throw a question or some code at the AI, and it gives you an answer and examples, but you have to paste the code over yourself. It's like the AI is a consultant, but you're still the one actually doing the work.
  • Type 3, AI Agent: You give it a task or a requirement, and it reads your project, decides which files to change, runs commands, and so on, only reporting back once it's done. In this setup you become the person who just gives orders (just like a boss). Tools like Claude Code and Codex fall into this type.

For now, all you need to know is that these three types exist, because the differences between them directly shape your Vibe Coding experience.

So... which one is Vibe Coding? Type 3, "AI Agent", of course.

With the first two you still have to touch the code yourself. Only an AI Agent is truly "you say it, it does it".

I refer to tools like Claude Code and Codex collectively as AI Agents.

A verification exercise

Tomorrow we're installing our AI Agent tool (Claude Code), but before that I want you to think about one question:

If you ask the AI to build an "add expense" feature, what does it take for it to actually be done?

Take some time to think this through, and please don't come up with something abstract like "you can enter an amount and submit it successfully". That's way too vague. You should list at least three or four conditions — things you can see and verify, like:

  • The form can't be submitted when the amount field is empty or 0
  • After adding a 120 lunch expense, the expense list immediately shows the entry you just added
  • After refreshing the page, the data is still there and doesn't disappear
  • On a phone-width screen, you can finish entering everything without scrolling sideways

Those are the smallest units for verifying a feature and a screen.

The idea is to write down "what I should see when it's done" before asking the AI to start working, so you avoid the situation where "it says it's done, but I have no idea what it actually did".

If you have an engineering background, you'll notice this is a lot like writing tests before writing code (TDD, Test Driven Development).

Why this series uses Claude Code

After all that, it's finally time to talk about why I picked Claude Code as the hands-on tool for this series.

It's pretty simple: Claude Code is arguably one of the best examples of what an AI Agent can be.

What do I mean? For example...

  1. You may have heard of MCP. It's an open protocol that Anthropic, the company behind Claude Code, released in 2024
  2. Skills and Subagents also came from Anthropic

Don't worry if none of those terms mean anything to you yet — they'll each show up in later posts. So as a hands-on tool for Vibe Coding, I think Claude Code is a pretty reasonable choice (and partly, sure, it's because it's the one I use the most).

If you already have an AI Agent tool you're comfortable with, that's fine too. AI companies all copy each other, and the Vibe Coding concepts themselves aren't tied to any tool. So even though I'm demoing with Claude Code, if you switch to Codex or Gemini later, the same ideas still apply.

Claude Code is one of Anthropic's official products. Others include the web version of Claude (claude.ai), Claude Desktop, and so on.

Also, Claude Code is probably the product engineers feel most at home with (I think?), since it runs right in the terminal and you can just talk to it naturally in your own language. The official docs describe how it works pretty plainly too. It first...

  1. Gathers context (reads your project, figures out where things stand)
  2. Then takes action (edits files, runs commands)
  3. Finally verifies the results (checks that what it built actually works)

To make it easier to picture, here's a quick Mermaid flowchart:

flowchart LR
    A["Gather context<br>Read the project, understand the current state"] --> B["Take action<br>Edit files, run commands"]
    B --> C["Verify results<br>Check that it works"]
    C -->|"Not there yet"| A
    C -->|"Done"| D["Report back to you"]

That's roughly what it looks like when it's working.

But notice one thing: whatever it does, it always leaves a record — which files it read, which section it changed, which commands it ran. How do you read those records? When should you tell it to stop? That's the fundamental skill we'll practice in later posts, where we'll be poking at every single line it changes.

Please stop asking me "why Claude Code and not XXX?" Once you've got the core Vibe Coding concepts down, the tools are all interchangeable.

Treat AI like a knowledgeable assistant or intern

We're almost at the end, and there's one last idea I want to leave you with:

Treat your AI Agent like a knowledgeable assistant or intern, not an all-knowing god. If you don't explain things clearly, all it can do is guess.

The point is this: if you hired an assistant to help you, you wouldn't just say "I want to build an expense tracker" and go to bed, right?

You'd explain the requirements clearly, break the big task down with them, check their work when they're done, and for the important core features you'd ask how they plan to do it, right?

Those communication and task-breakdown skills you'd use with an assistant or intern happen to be exactly what you need most for real-world Vibe Coding.

You'll find that every tool and every process over the next 28 days is really just putting that common sense into practice.

Flip it around: if you just toss out "I want to build an expense tracker" and go to bed, there's about an 80% chance you'll get something you didn't want. Then you'll call the AI dumb, and start wondering whether you're just not cut out for this. But really, you just didn't explain the requirements, didn't define what "done" looks like, and didn't break the task down.

Wrap-up

OK, last but not least, let's recap.

So what is Vibe Coding, really?

  • A way of building where you describe things in natural language and the AI does the coding. Andrej Karpathy coined it in 2025, and it got so big it became a Word of the Year.
  • Not needing to "write" code is true; not needing to "understand" is false. The skills you need shift from writing syntax to describing, verifying, and breaking things down.
  • Once you've got the core concepts down, you can do the real work with any AI Agent tool.
  • Treat AI like a knowledgeable assistant or intern, not an all-knowing god.

See you in the next post.

entry.title: 30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 1: The 30-Day Roadmap to Building an Expense Tracker App with Claude Code
entry.content:
Intro

Over the next 30 days, I'm going to use one single project to walk you through a complete, real-world Vibe Coding workflow.

Taking you from a fuzzy idea all the way to an expense tracker web app you can actually share with people.

The reason I wanted to write this series is that I've already written quite a few AI posts on my blog, but they're kind of scattered. If you're a beginner who wants to build your own little tool from zero, jumping from one post to another is honestly pretty painful. A lot of this stuff can't be covered by a single article — you have to go through an entire project yourself before it clicks when each piece actually shows up and gets used in real development.

So this series is one complete path, starting from the most basic of basic concepts.

For the next thirty days, I'll use Claude Code as the foundation and take you from basic operations all the way to building an expense tracker app (it doesn't have to be an expense tracker — feel free to build something else). We'll go step by step through the whole development process: requirements analysis, spec design, coding, debugging, UI design, and deployment.

You can apply these methods and techniques to Codex, Gemini, and other AI tools too, but the UI, commands, Permission Modes, Skills, and Hooks will differ a bit. Usually once you've got one AI tool down, you can pick up the others pretty quickly, because the concepts are similar and they mostly copy each other anyway.

Why learn by "building something"?

There's one thing I want to call out here. I've always felt that tool-focused tutorials have a ceiling. No matter how detailed the feature walkthrough is, it's hard for readers to understand where those features actually fit and when they come into play. And the tools keep updating on top of that, so it's always been a barrier.

I'm pretty sure you've had an experience like this at some point:

I understood everything in the article, but once I closed it and went back to my own project, I had no idea how to bring it in, when to use it, or even how to get started.

And honestly, I don't think that's your fault. Knowing a feature and knowing when to use which feature are two completely different things, and the second one only comes from real project experience.

So when I was planning the outline, I tried hard not to treat Claude Code as a feature-tour tool. Instead, the whole thing is built around developing a project, and I work backwards from there: what you should know, what concepts you should have, and how to actually operate things. I think that's way more practical than listing a pile of features, and it's less likely to go stale when the software updates. Along the way I'll also share some of my own thinking and principles.

So why did I pick Claude Code? I'm going to keep you in suspense on that one and save it for the next post. For now, all you need to know is that "this mindset works with any AI tool".

Even though this whole series revolves around Claude Code, I'll try to say "AI Agent" instead of "Claude Code" where I can, so it doesn't feel too locked into one specific tool. The point of this series is the concept of Vibe Coding, not any single tool, and that way you can take the same mindset to other AI tools too.

Hold on — please don't rush off and subscribe to an AI service yet. Wait until I cover it later; it's not too late then.

What will you have built after 30 days?

It might be a bit cliché, but I'm going to walk you through building your own expense tracker app (a web version). I'm calling it "Expense Tracker" (pretty straightforward, right?), and after 30 days you'll be able to share it with your friends.

So... what features are we planning?

  • Log an entry: Fill in the amount, category, date, and a note. Expenses and income live in two separate tabs.
  • This month's list: See everything you logged this month. Tap an entry to edit it, or delete it — with a confirmation before it's gone.
  • Category management: Add and delete your own categories, separately for expenses and income.
  • Monthly stats: See this month's total, plus the amount per category and a pie chart.
  • Budget alerts: Set a monthly budget, and when you go over, it shows how much you've overspent.
  • Data stays in your browser: Entries are stored in a little built-in storage area in your browser (called LocalStorage — more on it later). No separate database needed. Your data survives a refresh or closing the tab, but heads up: it won't carry over if you clear site data, switch browsers, or switch devices.
  • Works on phone and desktop: I'll show you some ways to guide the AI into building an RWD (Responsive Web Design) page, so it works on your phone, tablet, and computer.
  • Automation and going live: At the end we'll add a set of automated tests (so the code checks itself), and I'll show you how to use GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages to deploy it automatically. Don't worry if those two names mean nothing to you right now — when it's their turn, I'll explain them in plain language as best I can.

Sounds pretty good, right? But there's one idea I want to stress here:

This project isn't hard. The hard part isn't the features — it's getting the requirements right, getting the UI right, pulling the AI back when it drifts off course, and finishing the whole process so the thing actually ships.

So these thirty days aren't just about learning how to build something. You'll personally go through one full round of a Vibe Coding project: requirements, spec, development, debugging, UI design, all the way through testing and deployment until it's actually live.

On top of that, I'm deliberately leaving out login, cloud sync, export, and cross-month line charts in this series. That doesn't mean those features aren't important — I just want you to spend your energy on the process itself. You can always add features yourself later.

In the posts ahead, I'll keep bringing up "verification". It's not a Claude Code command, and it's not some kind of Mode. It means after the AI says "done", you have to try it out yourself and confirm the result actually matches what you originally asked for.

How the 30 days are laid out

Next, let me go over how I'm planning these 30 days. I've split the series into four weeks:

WeekThemeDaysProject progress
Week 1Concepts and basic operationsDay 1-7Get the basic concepts down
Week 2Kicking off the real build: from 0 to MVPDay 8-14Build a usable app from a spec
Week 3Skills week: better-looking UI + building your toolboxDay 15-21Use some Skills to overhaul the UI
Week 4Process week: turning the project into a productDay 22-28Set up a testing workflow and automate deployment
Wrap-upAll the pitfalls + recapDay 29-30Just a recap, plus some resources

One phase per week. I'm not going to make you deploy anything on day one, so relax.

What do I need to prepare?

You'll need...

  • A computer you can install software on (how are you going to Vibe Code without a computer?)
  • A GitHub account
  • A credit card (you'll need to buy an AI subscription later)
  • A little bit of English (don't worry if not — there are powerful translation tools to help you)

That's not everything, of course. Later on you'll also need to install Git, Node.js, and so on, but I'll walk you through installing those step by step in later posts.

"Do I need to know some code to Vibe Code?"

I'm pretty sure this is the thing people are most curious about. My answer is "no".

Knowing a little bit of code helps, but you don't need to be fluent, let alone be able to hand-write a feature yourself.

Of course, throughout this series I'll use plain language, diagrams, screenshots, and whatever else helps you understand and follow along. You'll still run into some technical terms here and there, since sometimes the technical term is just more precise — and I don't want other engineers rolling their eyes at me lol.

How long is each post? I'm aiming for about 15 to 30 minutes of reading, and the hands-on part might take anywhere from 45 to 90 minutes. That's just my personal feel, so adjust based on your own situation — it's only there to give you a rough expectation.

How do you know you're done for the day?

At the end of each post, I'll try to give you a way to check "what you should have in hand before the day is over". It might be a small challenge, a set of verification steps, or a screen you should be seeing.

Basically, just follow along with the post once. If things don't match up, go back through the article and check which steps you skipped or where something went wrong.

Also, the UI and the AI's text replies may differ depending on the model, so please don't try to match my screenshots exactly. AI is inherently random, and every output is different.

Who is this series for?

When planning this series, I had three kinds of readers in mind:

  1. Total beginners who've never touched AI: I'd suggest reading in order starting from Day 1. The whole series is designed for you, and each day builds on the previous one. I think it'll help you a lot with using AI.
  2. People already using AI: Week 1 will probably feel easy. Skim through it and see if there's anything you're not familiar with, then jump straight into Day 8 where the real build kicks off, or pick topics you haven't touched yet and dive in.
  3. Readers who don't plan to build anything right now: Totally fine to just watch this like a documentary of an AI dev project. I'll write down the decisions and the walls I hit along the way, and you should be able to take away quite a bit just from the process and the story.

Of course, what I really hope is that you build along with me. The soul of this series is the word "build".

Wrap-up

After all that, here's a quick recap:

  • I'll spend 30 days using AI to build an expense tracker web app from scratch and get it live
  • The four-week rhythm is... concepts and basics → real build to MVP → better-looking UI → process and deployment
  • Get a computer, a GitHub account, and a credit card ready, and set aside 45 to 90 minutes on hands-on days
  • Whether you're a total beginner, a seasoned user, or just here for the story, there's an entry point for you

I hope this post got you a little excited about the next 30 days, and I hope I actually make it to the finish line myself. Let's do this!

Tomorrow we'll talk about what the term "Vibe Coding" actually means and how it blew up, to lay the groundwork for the hands-on part.

See you on Day 2.

entry.title: What Are All Those .claude.json.tmp Files in My Home Directory? Can I Delete Them?
entry.content:
Intro

If you've been using Claude Code for a while, one day you'll open your Home directory to tidy things up and find a whole row of files that look like random junk:

.claude.json.tmp.3188.1774732246449
.claude.json.tmp.7114.1774839016660
.claude.json.tmp.44948.1774775486853
.claude.json.tmp.89591.1778114908901

In my case, I was clearing out disk space a while back and found 35 of them in one go. They don't take up much room, but they're annoying to look at — and honestly I didn't dare delete them at first. The name has .claude.json right there in it. What if they're part of the config?

Turns out you can delete them. But before you do, it's worth understanding what they are: who created them, why they stuck around, why Claude Code doesn't clean them up itself, and what's actually inside them. That way you won't hesitate or worry the next time you see them.

I've also written about Is Claude Code Auto Memory Hogging Your Memory? A Cleanup & Diagnostics Guide before — that one is about how conversation logs inside ~/.claude/ eat your disk. This post is about the neighbour one floor up, so the two go nicely together.

So what are those files?

Strictly speaking, these files shouldn't exist. They're temp files Claude Code left behind halfway through saving ~/.claude.json.

The names look like gibberish, but there's a pattern. Let me split one into four parts and it'll make a lot more sense:

.claude.json.tmp.3188.1774732246449

Each segment maps to the table below:

This partWhat it means
.claude.jsonThe target it was about to overwrite — Claude Code's global config file
tmpTemp file marker
3188The PID of the Claude Code process that created it
1774732246449A millisecond Unix timestamp recording when it was created

So what time does 1774732246449 actually work out to? Drop the last three digits (the milliseconds) and hand it to date. On macOS:

date -r 1774732246 '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'
# 2026-03-29 05:10:46

On Linux you'd use date -d @1774732246 instead.

Here's a small thing worth verifying while you're at it: the time you get back lines up with the file's modification time from ls -l.

Which means the filename alone tells you which day, and which Claude Code process, left the thing behind.

Why does saving a config file need a temp file at all?

Basically, to avoid ending up with a half-written config. There's a proper term for this approach — it's called an atomic write.

Atomic write? What's that?

Let me use a more everyday example. Say you want to overwrite an old version of a document with one you've just finished. The most intuitive approach is to open the old file, empty it, and type the new content in. But if the computer crashes halfway through typing, that file is now mangled — the new content never finished, and the old content isn't coming back.

To avoid that, Claude Code takes the "write to a temp file first, then rename over the old one" approach. The flow goes roughly like this:

  1. Write the complete new content into a brand-new temp file
  2. Apply the original config file's permissions to the temp file
  3. Use rename to rename the temp file to ~/.claude.json, overwriting it in one shot

In action, it looks something like this:

[DEBUG] Writing to temp file: ~/.claude.json.tmp.73914.1766019293909
[DEBUG] Preserving file permissions: 100644
[DEBUG] Temp file written successfully, size: 103774 bytes
[DEBUG] Applied original permissions to temp file
[DEBUG] Renaming ~/.claude.json.tmp.73914.1766019293909 to ~/.claude.json
[DEBUG] File written atomically

The upside is that if the write gets interrupted partway, the old config is still there and the new temp file is still there too. You can restart Claude Code and it'll run the write flow again — the config file never ends up corrupted.

So why do the leftovers stick around?

Simple: Claude Code got interrupted before it reached the rename step.

So the temp file just... ends up orphaned in your Home directory. The usual causes are:

  • Closing the terminal window outright
  • Hitting Ctrl + C to force-quit
  • The machine crashing, being force-rebooted, or force-logged-out

Before you delete them, you can also tell which step each one died at just from its size:

Leftover sizeWhere it died
0 bytesThe file had just been created and nothing had been written yet when it got interrupted, or the whole machine lost power before the data actually hit disk
Anywhere from 80 KB to 120 KBThe content was fully written — it just never got to that final rename

Of my 35, 20 were 0 bytes and 15 had content, so roughly a 60/40 split.

Why doesn't Claude Code clean them up itself?

Because Claude Code only cleans up things under ~/.claude/, and these temp file leftovers live one level up in the Home directory — out of reach. There is a built-in cleanupPeriodDays auto-cleanup mechanism (30 days by default), it just never sees them.

Files in the paths below are deleted on startup once they're older than cleanupPeriodDays. The default is 30 days.

Anthropic did address part of this, around v2.1.47:

Moved config backup files from home directory root to ~/.claude/backups/ to reduce home directory clutter

Config backups moved from the Home directory root into ~/.claude/backups/ — but the existing .tmp leftovers didn't move with them, which is why they're still sitting there. That part you have to clean up yourself.

How to check and clean them up

Let's go step by step. First, confirm how many you have and how much space they take:

ls -lh ~/.claude.json.tmp.* | wc -l
du -ch ~/.claude.json.tmp.* | tail -1

Next, batch-convert every timestamp into a readable date and sort them, so you can see when the most recent one was left behind:

for f in ~/.claude.json.tmp.*; do
  ts=${f##*.}
  printf '%s  %s\n' "$(date -r $((ts/1000)) '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M')" "$(basename "$f")"
done | sort

The output looks like this:

2026-03-29 05:10  .claude.json.tmp.3188.1774732246449
2026-03-29 17:11  .claude.json.tmp.44948.1774775486853
2026-03-30 10:50  .claude.json.tmp.7114.1774839016660
2026-04-01 02:56  .claude.json.tmp.6106.1774983410009

Once you've confirmed they're all old, if you're worried about slipping up you can do a dry run with echo first to see exactly which files would be touched:

for f in ~/.claude.json.tmp.*; do echo "rm $f"; done

If that looks right, delete them for real:

rm -f ~/.claude.json.tmp.*

That wildcard only matches files starting with .claude.json.tmp. — ~/.claude.json itself and ~/.claude.json.backup are both outside its range. That said, the official docs specifically warn against deleting ~/.claude.json, since your login state and preferences live in there. So when you're typing these commands manually, it's safer to read the line once more before hitting Enter.

After deleting, Claude Code carries on completely unaffected.

While we're here — meet the relatives

There are a few other similarly-named files in your Home directory and under ~/.claude/. Easier to keep them straight if we go through them together:

NameWhat it handlesSafe to delete?
~/.claude.jsonThe global config file itself — login state, preferences, and personal MCP servers all live hereDon't delete
~/.claude.json.tmp.<PID>.<timestamp>The star of this post — leftovers from an atomic write that never finishedYes
~/.claude.json.lockThe lock file used by that same write flow, so multiple sessions don't corrupt the config by writing at onceNormally disappears on its own; if one is left behind you can delete it
~/.claude.json.backupA config backup older versions left in the Home directory rootYes
~/.claude/backups/.claude.json.backup.<timestamp>The current backup mechanism — a snapshot taken before a config migrationYes. The official docs put it in the "deleting this loses nothing you can see" category

Hopefully this helps you get a feel for how Claude Code's config file gets written atomically, why it leaves temp file leftovers, why the auto-cleanup never catches them, and how to clear them out safely.

entry.title: Can't Find the Model You Want in Claude Code's /model Menu? Try This Trick
entry.content:
Intro

A new model just came out, but maybe you don't actually want to use it. Or maybe the model you do want isn't showing up when you run /model. Here's a small trick that lets you use the model you want in Claude Code anyway.

Claude Code's /model command

If you've used Claude Code, you probably already know that the /model command lets you switch models.

The list will usually give you options like these:

  1. Default (recommended): Opus5
  2. Opus (1M context): Opus5
  3. Fable
  4. Sonnet
  5. Opus 4.8

Most people will stick with Default (recommended): Opus5. But if you want to use a different model, you may run into a problem: the model you want simply isn't listed under /model.

The /model command only lists the models Claude Code officially recommends. Other available models won't appear in the menu.

Why does this happen? Basically, model providers want you on the version they recommend, since that's usually the most stable and best-supported option. So the other models stay hidden from the default list.

That can still be a problem, though. The most common reason is pretty simple:

The new model isn't as good as you expected.

Take Opus 4.8 as an example. Plenty of people felt that Opus 4.8 wasn't as good as Opus 4.6 or 4.7, so they preferred to keep using one of those older versions.

The trick: pass the model ID to /model

We're still using the /model command — we're just skipping the menu.

Say you want to use Opus 4.8. Open Claude Code and enter the following directly in the conversation:

/model claude-opus-4-8

The model ID has to be exact. You can find the available IDs in Anthropic's official Model Status documentation.

That page also tells you when each model will stop being supported. If the model you want has already reached end of support, you'll need to pick another one.

If you don't want a future Claude Code update to quietly change your model again, you can pin it in .claude/settings.json:

{
  "model": "claude-opus-4-8"
}

Keep the settings.json precedence in mind: system settings take priority over user settings.

And that's it — a small trick for keeping Claude Code on the model you actually want.
